items.title: Parquetry
items.text:
Parquetry reads and writes Apache Parquet and GeoParquet files from Java. Give it a file and a filter, and it returns the matching rows. The file can sit on a local disk, an HTTP server, Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage, and Parquetry fetches only the parts of it needed by the query. It runs inside long-lived servers with small container memory limits, such as GeoServer and GeoServer Cloud, and sizes its memory from that limit.

Why Parquetry? explains the deployment targeted by Parquetry, and when another tool fits better. Getting started adds Parquetry to a Java project and runs a first filtered read.

items.title: What you can do
items.text:
• Publish a GeoParquet file as a map layer

    Publish GeoParquet files from object storage or a mounted volume as vector layers of GeoServer Cloud, through its REST API. The Parquetry store is enabled by default.

    GeoParquet in GeoServer Cloud or GeoTools and GeoServer

  • Query a remote file by bounding box from Java

    Give a read a bounding box, and it returns the rows whose geometry has a bounding box overlapping it. The read fetches the parts of the file able to hold such rows, and leaves the rest on the server.

    Cloud storage then Filter by location

  • Hand a layer to an analytics engine

    Download a vector layer of GeoServer Cloud as a GeoParquet file or an Arrow IPC stream through WFS, and read it with DuckDB or with Python. From Java, Parquetry exports a read as Arrow.

    WFS output as GeoParquet and Arrow IPC or Arrow interop

items.title: Selective queries read little
items.text:
A Parquet file stores its rows in blocks called row groups. Inside a row group, the values of a column sit together in a column chunk, cut into pages. The footer at the end of the file describes the row groups and records the minimum and maximum of their column chunks. A page index, when the file has one, records the position, minimum and maximum of the pages. A bloom filter, when the file has one, tells whether a value may appear in a column chunk.

Parquetry reads this metadata before it fetches any data, and skips the parts of the file unable to match the filter. The diagram shows a small bounding box query on a file sorted by location.

flowchart TB
    subgraph file["A Parquet file"]
        direction TB
        subgraph rg1["Row group 1: ruled out by the footer"]
            r1["column chunks: skipped"]
        end
        subgraph rg2["Row group 2: kept"]
            direction LR
            subgraph r2c1["column chunk"]
                direction TB
                r2c1p1["page: skipped"]
                r2c1p2["page: fetched"]
                r2c1p3["page: skipped"]
            end
            subgraph r2c2["column chunk"]
                direction TB
                r2c2p1["page: skipped"]
                r2c2p2["page: fetched"]
                r2c2p3["page: skipped"]
            end
        end
        index["Page index and bloom filters"]
        footer["Footer: min/max of the column chunks"]
    end
    rg1 ~~~ rg2 ~~~ index ~~~ footer
    classDef skipped stroke-dasharray: 5 5
    classDef fetched stroke-width: 3px
    class r1,r2c1p1,r2c1p3,r2c2p1,r2c2p3 skipped
    class r2c1p2,r2c2p2 fetched

The levels run in this order:

  1. The statistics in the footer rule out row groups.
  2. The GeoParquet 2.0 geometry statistics, also in the footer, rule out the row groups whose geometries lie outside a bounding box.
  3. The page index rules out pages in the row groups left.
  4. Bloom filters rule out the row groups lacking the value of an eq or in filter.
  5. The read fetches the pages left, of the columns needed by the query, and tests their rows one by one. It returns the matching rows only.

A GeoParquet file written by Parquetry has a page index and bbox covering columns, four columns holding the bounding box of each geometry. For a small bounding box over such a file sorted by location, the statistics of the covering columns rule out the row groups far from the box. Their page index rules out the pages far from it in the row groups left, and the read fetches the few pages near the box.

The footer is read once per file. The page index and the bloom filters are read only for the row groups left by the levels before them. The levels work from the metadata of the file, and a file without it is pruned less. A read learns the pages of a file without a page index from their headers, and later reads of a row group prune pages with them (Without a page index). The per-row test keeps the result exact. Filter rows and Filter by location show the filters, and The read path follows a filtered read through these levels.

items.title: How it is built
items.text: Parquetry is a clean-room implementation of the Parquet format in Java: it depends on neither Hadoop nor parquet-java, and it runs no native engine. It reads files through tileverse-storage, and its architecture diagrams show the modules and how a read flows through them. Format support lists the Parquet and GeoParquet features read and written by Parquetry.

items.title: Status
items.text:
Parquetry has not reached 1.0, and its API may still change before then. The stable parts are ready for production use. The experimental parts work, but their behavior is still changing.

Area Module Status Reading Parquet files, with filter pushdown parquetry-core stable Writing Parquet files, Parquet 2.0 by default and 1.1 on request parquetry-core stable GeoParquet 1.x and 2.0 metadata, spatial filtering parquetry-core stable Multi-file datasets: a directory or a glob of files read as one dataset parquetry-catalog stable GeoTools data store for GeoParquet parquetry-geotools stable Export to Arrow: Arrow IPC streams and the Arrow C Data Interface parquetry-arrow stable Reading Apache Iceberg tables parquetry-iceberg experimental Reading STAC GeoParquet collections parquetry-stac experimental The par command line tool par experimental

Two supporting modules have no status of their own. parquetry-avro reads and writes Avro container files, the format of Iceberg manifests and manifest lists. parquetry-jackson renders the rows of a read as JSON.

items.title: In GeoServer Cloud
items.text:
GeoServer Cloud 3.1.0 and newer include Parquetry (GeoServer Cloud). The Parquetry extension, its "Parquet" data store, and the geoparquet and arrow-ipc WFS output formats are enabled by default. The Iceberg and STAC GeoParquet stores are not ready for production yet, and ship disabled. The GeoServer Cloud user guide covers both uses:

  • GeoParquet through the REST API publishes GeoParquet files as layers.
  • WFS output as GeoParquet and Arrow IPC downloads any vector layer as a GeoParquet file or an Arrow IPC stream, regardless of its store.

items.title: Part of the Tileverse ecosystem
items.text: Parquetry is part of Tileverse, a set of Java libraries for cloud-native geospatial applications. Its storage layer, tileverse-storage, provides the byte-range reads and the caches used by Parquetry.

items.title: Getting started
items.text: You have a Java 25 project and a Parquet file, and want the rows matching a condition. This page adds Parquetry to a Maven project and runs a short program printing the countries of a sample file with at least 100 million inhabitants. The latest release is 1.0-RC6, published on Maven Central.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
Parquetry requires Java 25. The modules using preview features run on Java 25 only, and parquetry-core also runs on newer versions. Start the JVM of your application with these two flags:

java --enable-preview --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED -jar your-application.jar
  • --enable-preview is required by the modules compiled with Java 25 preview features. parquetry-catalog is one of them, and the GeoTools data store depends on it. A JVM started without the flag refuses to load these classes. These modules run on Java 25 only: a Java 26 JVM refuses their classes, even with the flag. parquetry-core alone has no such classes, and also runs on Java 26.
  • --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED lets Parquetry allocate its native buffers as memory mappings. Without it, the JDK prints a warning at the first mapping. Memory explains why Parquetry maps its buffers.

Give the same flags to the JVM running your tests, for example in the argLine of the Maven Surefire plugin.

items.title: Add the dependency
items.text:
Import the Parquetry BOM, then declare the modules needed by your code without a version. parquetry-core reads and writes single Parquet and GeoParquet files:

<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>io.tileverse.parquetry</groupId>
      <artifactId>parquetry-bom</artifactId>
      <version>1.0-RC6</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>io.tileverse.parquetry</groupId>
    <artifactId>parquetry-core</artifactId>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

The BOM pins the versions of the Parquetry modules. To also pin the third-party libraries used by Parquetry, such as tileverse-storage and JTS, import io.tileverse.parquetry:parquetry-dependencies the same way. Modules lists the published modules and the two BOMs.

items.title: Read a file
items.text:
The example reads the sample file of the GeoParquet specification, a few countries with their population and their geometry. Download it as countries.parquet:

curl -L -o countries.parquet https://github.com/opengeospatial/geoparquet/raw/v2.0.0/examples/example.parquet

The program prints the countries with at least 100 million inhabitants:

import static io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Pred.col;

import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ParquetFileReader;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ReadOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Projection;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.io.ByteRangeSource;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.record.ParquetRecord;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ColumnPath;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class FirstRead {

    private static final ColumnPath NAME = ColumnPath.of("name");
    private static final ColumnPath POPULATION = ColumnPath.of("pop_est");

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Path path = Path.of("countries.parquet");
        Predicate filter = col("pop_est").gtEq(100_000_000.0);
        Projection columns = Projection.ofPhysical(List.of(NAME, POPULATION));

        try (ByteRangeSource source = ByteRangeSource.ofFile(path)) {
            ParquetFileReader reader = ParquetFileReader.open(source);
            try (Stream<ParquetRecord> rows = reader.read(filter, columns, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS)) {
                rows.forEach(FirstRead::printCountry);
            }
        }
    }

    private static void printCountry(ParquetRecord row) {
        String name = row.getString(NAME);
        double population = row.getDouble(POPULATION);
        System.out.println(name + ": " + population);
    }
}

It prints United States of America: 3.28239523E8. The example follows the usual shape of a read:

  • ByteRangeSource.ofFile opens the file. The source owns the open file, and closing it releases the file.
  • ParquetFileReader.open reads the footer of the file. The reader is safe to share between threads.
  • read takes three arguments: a predicate selecting the rows, a projection selecting the columns, and the read options. It returns a lazy stream of rows. Close the stream when you are done with it, to release the buffers of the read.
  • The predicate is evaluated inside the read. Parquetry uses it to skip the row groups and pages that cannot match, and returns only the matching rows. A row group is a block of rows of the file, and a page is a smaller run of values of one column inside it.

To read the whole file, pass Predicate.ALWAYS_TRUE and Projection.ALL.

Read the values of a row while the stream hands it to you. A row is a view over a batch of decoded rows, and the batch closes as the stream moves on. The typed get accessors, such as getString and getDouble, return values that you can keep. Call detach() on a row to keep the row itself.

items.title: Why Parquetry?
items.text:
A GeoServer pod serves maps from a large GeoParquet file on object storage, with a container memory limit of a few gigabytes. Under load, the requests in flight use more memory together than the limit allows. The kernel kills the pod, and those requests fail while it restarts.

Java applications can already read Parquet. parquet-java is the Java implementation maintained by the Apache Parquet project, and Java code can query Parquet files with DuckDB through its JDBC driver. Parquetry exists for one deployment: a long-lived Java server, often GeoServer, serving GeoParquet from a container with a small memory limit. This page lists the constraints of that deployment, to help you decide whether they match yours.

items.title: The audience
items.text:
Parquetry is built for a specific class of application:

  • Long-lived servers. GeoServer, GeoServer Cloud and other GeoTools-based services run for days and answer many requests at the same time. A reader is opened once and shared by concurrent requests.
  • Containers with small memory limits. GeoServer Cloud is the reference deployment. Its pods run with a few gigabytes of memory, and a scheduler sets their memory limits.
  • Many datasets in one process. One server publishes many layers, and a layer reads its own files.
  • Files on object storage. GeoParquet files sit on Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage or an HTTP server. A map request needs a small part of a file, and the reader fetches it with byte-range requests.
  • The GeoTools and GeoServer ecosystem. Geometries are JTS geometries, a layer is served by a GeoTools data store, and the dependency tree has no Hadoop.

If your workload does not share these constraints, Parquetry may not be the right tool: see When not to use Parquetry.

items.title: The constraints of that deployment
items.text:
The container limit counts all memory. The JVM heap limit (-Xmx) covers only the heap. The container limit counts the heap, the native memory of the process, and everything else. When the process crosses the container limit, the kernel kills it with a signal. No OutOfMemoryError is thrown, no request gets an error response, and the requests in flight are lost while the container restarts.

One limit for the whole process. The container enforces one limit on the sum of the memory used by the layers. A limit set per layer does not bound that sum. An operator would have to split the container memory between the layers by hand, and redo the split when a layer is added.

The pod size changes. A scheduler can give pods different memory limits. A setting computed by hand for a 4 GB pod is too large for a 2 GB pod and wastes most of a 16 GB pod.

Many requests read the same files at once. A request must not hold its own copy of the file metadata. A reader that parses the footer of a file once per request multiplies its memory by the number of concurrent requests.

Remote bytes are slow and cost money. A request for a small area of a large file must not download the file. The reader must decide which parts of the file it needs before it fetches them.

items.title: What Parquetry does about them
items.text:
It sizes its memory from the container limit. At startup, Parquetry reads the memory limit of the container and derives its native memory budgets from the memory left beside the heap. Readers share these budgets. Adding a layer adds nothing to tune, and a pod of another size gets budgets scaled to its own limit. Memory describes the budgets and their defaults.

A full budget slows a read down instead of killing the process. When the fetch budget is full, a read waits for other reads to release room, up to one second by default. If no room frees up in that time, the read writes its buffers to a memory-mapped temporary file. When the disk budget is full too, the read fails with an exception, and the other requests keep running. Native memory and spill explains the spill path.

It decodes Parquet in the JVM. Parquetry runs no native query engine beside the JVM. A layer does not get an engine instance with a memory pool of its own. It depends on neither Hadoop nor parquet-java.

It shares file metadata between readers. A reader parses the footer of a file once and keeps a compact form of it. Readers opened on the same file share that form, and a reader is safe to share between threads.

It fetches only the byte ranges needed by a query. Parquetry discards the row groups and pages that cannot match the filter, using column statistics, GeoParquet bounding boxes, page indexes and bloom filters. It fetches the remaining data with byte-range requests through tileverse-storage, from a local disk, an HTTP server or object storage (Cloud storage). The read path walks through a filtered read, and Spatial filtering covers bounding box and geometry filters.

items.title: Background
items.text: The author of Parquetry also wrote the DuckDB-based GeoParquet store for GeoTools and GeoServer. That store still exists, and GeoServer Cloud runs it side by side with the Parquetry store. DuckDB 2.0 bounds the buffer memory of an engine instance with its memory_limit setting, and its threads with the threads setting. The documentation of the GeoParquet community module for GeoServer 3.0.x lists both settings as parameters of a store. Those limits work within one engine instance. A server with many stores runs many instances, and the operator has to split the container memory between them by hand. Parquetry was started for the deployment where one container hosts many stores and a scheduler assigns its memory limit.

items.title: When not to use Parquetry
items.text:
Pick something else when:

  • You work inside a Spark or Hadoop pipeline. Use parquet-java, the Parquet implementation used by Spark and by the Hadoop ecosystem. Spark 4.3.0 reads Parquet through parquet-java 1.17.0.
  • You run SQL analytics over Parquet files. Joins, aggregations and ad hoc queries belong to an analytics engine such as DuckDB. Parquetry is not a query engine. It can feed one: its Arrow IPC output gives an engine columnar input, and the arrow-ipc WFS output format of GeoServer Cloud does the same for any vector layer.
  • You work in Python. Use pyarrow, the Python library of Apache Arrow: pyarrow 26.0.1 reads and writes Parquet files. GeoPandas 1.2.0 reads and writes GeoParquet through pyarrow.
  • Your application runs on Java 24 or older. Parquetry needs Java 25. The multi-file datasets and the GeoTools data store use preview features of Java 25, and run on that version only. Getting started lists the requirements.

items.title: The par command line tool
items.text:
Experimental

par works, but its commands, options and output may change between releases.

You have a Parquet or GeoParquet file and want to see its schema, its metadata and a few rows without writing code. par prints them from the command line, filters rows with a SQL WHERE expression, and copies files into a new layout. It reads local files, files on object storage, directories of files and Apache Iceberg tables.

items.title: Build par
items.text:
par is not published as a download. It builds from the source repository, with JDK 25:

git clone https://github.com/tileverse-io/parquetry.git
cd parquetry
./mvnw -pl :par -am package -DskipTests

The build writes a self-contained jar, apps/par/target/par-<version>-shaded.jar. The script apps/par/bin/par runs that jar with the JVM flags required by Parquetry, --enable-preview and --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED (Getting started explains both). The environment variable JAVA_OPTS passes more JVM options to the script, such as -Xmx2g.

Put the script on your PATH, or define an alias:

alias par="$PWD/apps/par/bin/par"
par --help

It prints the commands:

Usage: par [OPTIONS] COMMAND
Inspect and transform Parquet files.
  -h, --help      Show this help message and exit.
  -V, --version   Print version information and exit.
Commands:
  schema               Print the Parquet message-type tree of a file,
                         directory, or Iceberg table.
  meta                 Print a one-screen file summary.
  cat                  Decode rows of a file, directory, or Iceberg table to
                         stdout (jsonl by default).
  head                 Decode the first rows of a file, directory, or Iceberg
                         table to stdout (jsonl by default).
  cp                   Read src, apply projection/filter, write a new Parquet
                         file at dst.
  explain              Print the file-pruning and scan plan for a Parquet file,
                         directory, or Iceberg table.
  row-groups           List the file's row groups.
  row-count            Print the number of rows in a Parquet file.
  stats                Print per-column statistics.
  generate-completion  Generate bash/zsh completion script for par.

par <command> without arguments prints the options of that command, after a line naming the missing argument.

items.title: Look at a file
items.text:
The examples on these pages use the sample file of the GeoParquet specification, saved as countries.parquet as in Getting started. par schema prints the columns and their types:

$ par schema countries.parquet
message schema {
  optional DOUBLE pop_est;
  optional BYTE_ARRAY continent (StringType);
  optional BYTE_ARRAY name (StringType);
  optional BYTE_ARRAY iso_a3 (StringType);
  optional INT64 gdp_md_est;
  optional BYTE_ARRAY geometry (Geometry);
  optional group bbox {
    optional DOUBLE xmax;
    optional DOUBLE xmin;
    optional DOUBLE ymax;
    optional DOUBLE ymin;
  }
}

par meta summarizes the footer, the metadata stored at the end of the file. A row group is a block of rows described in the footer:

$ par meta countries.parquet
created by:     parquet-cpp-arrow version 20.0.0
format version: 2
rows:           5
row groups:     1
leaf columns:   10
uncompressed:   23719 bytes
compressed:     21777 bytes
key-value:      ARROW:schema, geo

par head prints the first rows, ten by default, as one JSON object per line. --columns keeps some columns, and --limit sets the number of rows:

$ par head countries.parquet --columns name,pop_est --limit 3
{"pop_est":889953.0,"name":"Fiji"}
{"pop_est":5.8005463E7,"name":"Tanzania"}
{"pop_est":603253.0,"name":"W. Sahara"}

The columns come in the order of the file, not the order of --columns. A nested column is named by its path, such as --columns bbox.xmin.

items.title: The commands
items.text:
Command What it prints or does par schema <uri> The schema of the file, as a Parquet message type. par meta <uri> A summary of the footer: writer, rows, row groups, sizes, key-value metadata. par head <uri> The first rows, ten unless --limit says otherwise. par cat <uri> The rows. par row-count <uri> The number of rows, or of matching rows with --filter. par row-groups <uri> The row groups, with their rows and sizes. par stats <uri> The statistics of the column chunks: value and null counts, minimum, maximum. par explain <uri> The parts of the file skipped by a filter (Filter rows). par cp <src> <dst> A new Parquet file, with a subset of the rows and columns (Copy files). par generate-completion A completion script for bash and zsh.

A column chunk holds the values of one column within one row group. par stats prints one line per column chunk:

$ par stats countries.parquet
rowGroup  column                type                        values       nulls               min               max
--------  --------------------  ----------------------  ----------  ----------  ----------------  ----------------
0         pop_est               DOUBLE                           5           0          603253.0      3.28239523E8
0         continent             BYTE_ARRAY                       5           0            Africa           Oceania
0         name                  BYTE_ARRAY                       5           0            Canada         W. Sahara

The output above is cut after three lines. par stats prints the minimum and maximum of a binary column as raw bytes. For a geometry column, these bytes print as unreadable text.

items.title: Options of the row commands
items.text:
cat, head, cp, explain and row-count take these options:

Option Meaning --columns <col>[,<col>...] The leaf columns to keep, separated by commas. All columns by default. --filter <sql> A SQL WHERE expression, applied inside the read (Filter rows). --filter-help Print the supported --filter expressions and exit. --limit <n> The maximum number of rows printed, or written by cp. -o, --format <format> The output format. -v, --verbose Print the full stack trace of an error.

items.title: Output formats
items.text:
-o takes a different set of formats for each command. The names are case-insensitive.

  • cat and head print jsonl by default, one JSON object per line. They also print csv, tsv, text and arrow.
  • schema, meta, explain, row-groups and stats print text by default, and json.
  • row-count prints a plain number.
$ par cat countries.parquet --columns name,continent,pop_est -o csv
pop_est,continent,name
889953.0,Oceania,Fiji
5.8005463E7,Africa,Tanzania
603253.0,Africa,W. Sahara
3.7589262E7,North America,Canada
3.28239523E8,North America,United States of America

In jsonl, a list prints as a JSON array, and a struct or a map as a JSON object. A Parquet Variant column prints as its JSON value. In csv, tsv and text, a nested column prints as one cell of compact JSON. A binary column without a string type, such as a WKB geometry, prints as Base64 text.

-o arrow writes an Arrow IPC stream to standard output, for a tool reading Arrow, such as DuckDB, Polars or pandas. Geometry columns are tagged as geoarrow.wkb. With DuckDB 2.0.0 and its nanoarrow community extension:

$ par cat countries.parquet --columns name,continent,pop_est -o arrow \
    | duckdb -csv -c "install nanoarrow from community; load nanoarrow;
        select continent, count(*) as n from read_arrow('/dev/stdin')
        group by continent order by continent"
continent,n
Africa,2
North America,2
Oceania,1

Arrow interop lists how the Parquet types map to Arrow types.

items.title: Read from object storage
items.text:
The <uri> argument is a local path or a URI. Its scheme selects the storage backend:

  • a path, or file://, for a local file;
  • s3://bucket/key for Amazon S3 and S3-compatible services;
  • gs://bucket/key for Google Cloud Storage;
  • az://account/container/blob, or an https://account.blob.core.windows.net/... URL, for Azure Blob Storage, and abfs:// or abfss:// for Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2;
  • http:// or https:// for a server answering range requests.

par includes the backends listed in Cloud storage. Without options, a backend looks for credentials in its usual places, such as environment variables and configuration files. These options set them on the command line:

Option Meaning --provider <id> Force the backend: s3, gcs, azure, http or file. --region <region> The S3 region. --access-key <key>, --secret-key <key> The S3 credentials. --path-style S3 path-style addressing, as required by MinIO and other S3-compatible services. --endpoint <url> The endpoint of S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure, such as http://localhost:9000 for a local MinIO. --gcs-project <project> The Google Cloud project. --anonymous Read without credentials, for a public bucket.

items.title: Read directories and Iceberg tables
items.text:
schema, cat, head, row-count and explain read more than one file as one dataset:

  • For a local directory, par reads the .parquet files below it, subdirectories included. The files must have the same schema.
  • For a glob, such as 'data/*.parquet', par reads the matching files. Quote it to keep the shell from expanding it.
  • A remote URI ending in / is a prefix. par reads the .parquet files below it.
  • A directory or a prefix holding metadata/*.metadata.json is an Apache Iceberg table. par reads its current snapshot (Apache Iceberg tables).

meta, row-groups, stats and cp read one file. Multi-file datasets describes how a dataset reads its files.

items.title: Exit codes
items.text:
Code Meaning 0 Success. 1 Another error, such as a missing file or an unknown column. 2 Wrong arguments or an unknown option. 3 A schema error, such as two files of a directory with different schemas. 4 A malformed file, or a feature of the file not supported by Parquetry. 5 A --filter expression rejected by par, such as an unsupported function.

An error prints as par: <message> on standard error. -v adds the stack trace.

items.title: Shell completion
items.text:
par generate-completion prints a completion script for bash, also usable from zsh:

# bash, current shell
source <(par generate-completion)

# zsh, current shell
autoload -Uz compinit && compinit
autoload -Uz bashcompinit && bashcompinit
source <(par generate-completion)

items.title: Copy files with par
items.text:
Experimental

par works, but its commands, options and output may change between releases.

You have a Parquet or GeoParquet file and want a new file from it: some of its rows and columns, a layout better suited to selective queries, or a copy in another store. par cp reads the source with the columns and the filter given, and writes a new Parquet file with Parquetry's writer. Lay out files for selective queries gives the recipe for the layout, with par cp.

items.title: Copy some rows and columns
items.text:
With countries.parquet from Getting started, this command keeps the African countries and three columns:

$ par cp countries.parquet africa.parquet --columns name,pop_est,geometry --filter "continent = 'Africa'"
$ par cat africa.parquet --columns name,pop_est
{"pop_est":5.8005463E7,"name":"Tanzania"}
{"pop_est":603253.0,"name":"W. Sahara"}

--columns, --filter and --limit work as in the other commands (Filter rows). The filter can name a column left out of the copy, such as continent here.

The copy is a GeoParquet file. par cp writes new GeoParquet metadata for the columns of the copy, and copies the other key-value metadata of the source. It also adds bbox columns, the covering of GeoParquet 1.1: four columns holding the bounding boxes of the geometries, used by readers to skip data under a spatial filter.

$ par schema africa.parquet
message schema {
  optional DOUBLE pop_est;
  optional BYTE_ARRAY name (StringType);
  optional BYTE_ARRAY geometry (Geometry);
  optional group bbox {
    optional FLOAT xmin;
    optional FLOAT ymin;
    optional FLOAT xmax;
    optional FLOAT ymax;
  }
}

The bbox columns hold FLOAT values for a geometry column in longitude and latitude (CRS84 or EPSG:4326), and DOUBLE values otherwise.

par cp copies struct, list, map and Variant columns. It rejects a column of the legacy INT96 type with exit code 4, as in this file of the Apache parquet-testing repository. --columns can leave that column out:

$ par cp alltypes_plain.parquet copy.parquet
par: cp cannot write INT96 column 'timestamp_col'

items.title: Choose the destination
items.text:
The destination is a local path or a URI, with the schemes of Read from object storage.

  • A destination ending in /, or an existing local directory, receives a file named after the source.

  • An existing destination stops the copy, unless -f or --overwrite is given:

    $ par cp countries.parquet countries-copy.parquet
par: destination exists (use -f to overwrite): countries-copy.parquet

  • The writer keeps its working files in the system temporary directory. --temp-dir <dir> puts them elsewhere, for example when that volume is small or read-only.

The source and the destination can sit in two different stores. The storage options of Read from object storage apply to the source. The destination has its own, with the --dst- prefix:

Option Meaning --dst-provider <id> Force the backend of the destination: s3, gcs, azure, http or file. --dst-region <region> The S3 region of the destination. --dst-access-key <key>, --dst-secret-key <key> The S3 credentials of the destination. --dst-path-style S3 path-style addressing for the destination. --dst-endpoint <url> The endpoint of S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure for the destination. --dst-gcs-project <project> The Google Cloud project of the destination. --dst-anonymous Write to the destination without credentials.

items.title: Change the layout
items.text:
These options change the layout of the copy. Lay out files for selective queries explains the choices and the order of the rows.

Option Meaning --row-group-bytes <size> Close a row group at about this size of uncompressed data, such as 256MB. The units K, M and G are binary. --row-group-rows <n> Close a row group after n rows. --covering-page-values <n> The number of values in a page of the bbox columns, 1024 by default. The other columns keep the page size of the writer. --float-column-order <order> The order of the statistics of FLOAT, DOUBLE and FLOAT16 columns: type_defined, the default, or ieee_754_total_order (Choose the order of float statistics).

A row group is a block of rows described in the footer of the file. A page is a part of a column within a row group, and the unit skipped by the page index. Without --row-group-bytes or --row-group-rows, row groups hold about 128 MB of uncompressed data.

items.title: Choose the GeoParquet metadata
items.text:
--geoparquet-metadata <version> sets the GeoParquet metadata of the copy:

  • dual, the default: native geometry types and a 1.1.0 geo document, readable by GeoParquet 1.x and 2.0 readers;
  • 2.0: native geometry types and a 2.0.0 document;
  • 1.1: a 1.1.0 document only.

--bbox-covering <mode> decides the bbox columns of a copy whose source declares no covering: auto, the default, float, double or none.

With auto, a bbox struct already in the source becomes the covering of the copy. DuckDB writes such a struct without declaring it in the metadata. The sample file has one, with its fields in the order xmax, xmin, ymax, ymin. The copy declares it, and writes the fields in the order required by GeoParquet 1.1:

$ par cp countries.parquet countries-copy.parquet
$ par schema countries-copy.parquet
message schema {
  ...
  optional group bbox {
    optional DOUBLE xmin;
    optional DOUBLE ymin;
    optional DOUBLE xmax;
    optional DOUBLE ymax;
  }
}

The struct must follow these rules:

  • Its fields are xmin, ymin, xmax and ymax, with zmin and zmax optional, and no other.
  • Its fields are all FLOAT or all DOUBLE.
  • It has the repetition of the geometry column.

If the struct breaks a rule, the copy declares no covering, and par prints the reason. Without a bbox struct, auto derives new bbox columns, as in the African copy above. float and double force the type of derived columns, and none writes no covering.

A covering declared by the source is kept whatever the flag says, under the same rules. When the copy cannot keep it, par prints the reason and follows the flag.

items.title: Filter rows with par
items.text:
Experimental

par works, but its commands, options and output may change between releases.

You want the rows matching a condition, such as the countries of a continent or the features inside a box, without writing code. --filter takes a SQL WHERE expression and applies it inside the read: par skips the parts of the file unable to match, and tests the remaining rows one by one. par explain shows what was skipped.

items.title: Filter a read
items.text:
cat, head, row-count, explain and cp take --filter. With countries.parquet from Getting started:

$ par cat countries.parquet --columns name,pop_est --filter "pop_est > 50000000"
{"pop_est":5.8005463E7,"name":"Tanzania"}
{"pop_est":3.28239523E8,"name":"United States of America"}
$ par row-count countries.parquet --filter "pop_est > 50000000"
2

The columns of the filter need not be among the columns printed:

$ par cat countries.parquet --columns name,iso_a3 \
    --filter "continent = 'Africa' OR pop_est BETWEEN 1000000 AND 40000000"
{"name":"Tanzania","iso_a3":"TZA"}
{"name":"W. Sahara","iso_a3":"ESH"}
{"name":"Canada","iso_a3":"CAN"}

items.title: The expressions
items.text:
--filter-help prints the supported expressions. In short:

Kind Expressions Comparisons = != <> < <= > >= Logic AND, OR, NOT, parentheses Sets and ranges IN (...), NOT IN (...), BETWEEN x AND y, IS NULL, IS NOT NULL Spatial relations ST_Intersects, ST_Touches, ST_Crosses, ST_Overlaps, ST_Disjoint, ST_Equals, ST_Contains, ST_Within, ST_Covers, ST_CoveredBy, ST_DWithin Query geometries ST_GeomFromText('<WKT>'), ST_MakeEnvelope(minx, miny, maxx, maxy) Bounding boxes ST_Extent(<geometry column>), ST_Envelope(<geometry column>)

The rules:

  • The left side of a comparison is a column. The right side is a literal: a number, a 'string', true or false.
  • A null value matches no comparison, and no negation of a comparison: x <> 1, NOT (x = 1) and x NOT IN (1) skip it. IS NULL selects it.
  • A column named after a SQL keyword, or with a space in its name, goes in double quotes: "from" > 1, "my column" = 2. A double quote inside the name is written twice: "a""b" = 4.
  • A filter on a nested column names its path, such as "outer".code = 3.

An expression outside this list fails with exit code 5:

$ par cat countries.parquet --filter "upper(name) = 'FIJI'"
par: unsupported in --filter: upper (run with --filter-help to list the supported predicates)

items.title: Filter by location
items.text:
The spatial functions test the exact geometries of the rows against a query geometry:

$ par cat countries.parquet --columns name \
    --filter "ST_Intersects(geometry, ST_MakeEnvelope(-100, 30, -90, 40))"
{"name":"United States of America"}
$ par cat countries.parquet --columns name \
    --filter "ST_DWithin(geometry, ST_GeomFromText('POINT(178 -17)'), 2)"
{"name":"Fiji"}
  • The tests run in the coordinate reference system of the file. par does not reproject the query geometry: write its coordinates in that system.
  • ST_Contains and ST_Within, and ST_Covers and ST_CoveredBy, depend on the order of their arguments. ST_Within(geometry, <query>) keeps the rows inside the query geometry.
  • ST_DWithin takes a distance as its third argument, in the units of the coordinates.

ST_Extent(geometry) stands for the bounding box of the geometry. With it, the test compares two rectangles and skips the exact geometry test. Edges count as inside, and Z is ignored:

$ par cat countries.parquet --columns name \
    --filter "ST_Intersects(ST_Extent(geometry), ST_MakeEnvelope(-100, 30, -90, 40))"
{"name":"United States of America"}

The rectangle form accepts ST_Intersects, ST_Covers, ST_CoveredBy, ST_Equals and ST_Disjoint, and a query written as ST_MakeEnvelope, ST_Extent or ST_Envelope. The other relations reject it and say what to use instead:

$ par cat countries.parquet \
    --filter "ST_Contains(ST_Extent(geometry), ST_MakeEnvelope(-20, 20, -10, 30))"
par: ST_Contains has no bounding-box form: box relations include their edges, and a geometry on the query edge answers differently under ST_Contains; use ST_Covers for the box relation, or remove ST_Extent(geometry) to test the exact geometry (run with --filter-help to list the supported predicates)

ST_Envelope is a synonym of ST_Extent. It is the spelling understood by PostGIS for the box of one geometry, where ST_Extent aggregates over rows.

Filter by location explains the same tests in the Java API.

items.title: See what a filter skips
items.text:
par explain prints the decisions taken on the metadata of the file, without reading the rows. A Parquet file keeps its rows in row groups, blocks of rows described in the footer at the end of the file. The sample file has a single row group. This copy splits it into row groups of two rows (Copy files):

par cp countries.parquet countries-rg.parquet --row-group-rows 2

The copy also has bbox columns, holding the bounding boxes of the geometries. A spatial filter uses their statistics to skip row groups:

$ par explain countries-rg.parquet \
    --filter "ST_Intersects(geometry, ST_MakeEnvelope(-100, 30, -90, 40))"
predicate: GeometryFilterPredicate[filter=io.tileverse.parquetry.geo.JtsGeometryFilter@76a36b71]
1 kept, 0 skipped  (0 rows pruned without opening a file)

location                                 outcome         rows   reason
countries-rg.parquet                     KEEP               5   kept

countries-rg.parquet:
Tiers: STATS, SPATIAL, COLUMN_INDEX, BLOOM_FILTER, RECORD_LEVEL
RG  Rows  Stats  Spatial  ColIdx  Bloom  Record  Outcome
0   2     ELIM   -        -       -      -       skip   
1   2     n/a    n/a      passed  n/a    -       all    
2   1     n/a    n/a      passed  n/a    -       all

The first line shows the filter as Parquetry received it. The file table comes next: for a directory or an Iceberg table, it lists the files, kept or skipped with the reason. The last table has one line per row group of a kept file, and one column per tier, in the order of the read:

  • Stats: the minimum and maximum of the column chunks, from the footer. Row group 0 holds Fiji and Tanzania, far from the query box, and its bbox statistics rule it out.
  • Spatial: the bounding box of the geometries of the row group, recorded in the footer of files with native geometry types, such as GeoParquet 2.0 files.
  • ColIdx: the page index. A column chunk is cut into pages, and the page index records the minimum and maximum of the pages. It skips pages inside a row group.
  • Bloom: the bloom filters, compact sets answering whether a value may be present in a column chunk.
  • Record: the test of the rows one by one. explain reads no rows, and prints -.

A cell holds ELIM when the tier ruled the row group out, NARROW n/m when it kept n rows out of m, kept or passed when the row group went on, and n/a when the tier had no data or did not apply. A - follows an ELIM: the later tiers did not run. The Outcome column gives the result: skip, all for rows still to test, matched when the statistics proved that all rows match, or a number of rows left.

--analyze runs the read as well, and adds per row group the rows matched, the bytes read and the time spent, then the totals and the requests sent to storage. -o json prints the plan as JSON.

Lay out files for selective queries shows how the order of the rows and the page size make these tiers skip more.

items.text:
• The read path describes the tiers.
  • Spatial filtering explains how the bbox columns and the bounds of GeoParquet 2.0 files skip row groups and pages.

items.title: Counting
items.text:
In short

count returns the number of matching rows without building them. Where the metadata proves that none or all of the rows of a row group match, it answers without decoding; elsewhere it decodes the filter columns only and counts the matches. It returns the same number as counting the rows of a read.

This page explains how count(predicate) returns the number of matching rows without materializing them, and why it costs much less than reading the rows. It is for developers counting rows, for example the feature count of a GeoTools layer.

Counting reuses the filter pipeline and the row-group outcomes described in The read path.

The guiding rule: count proves what it can from statistics and counts the rest with a columnar popcount: it never materializes a record. A read().count() decodes the surviving rows into ParquetRecord objects only to drop them. count() does none of that.

items.title: 1. What count is
items.text:
ParquetFileReader.count(predicate, options) returns how many rows satisfy predicate. It is the answer to a GeoTools getCount(Query), a SELECT count(*) WHERE ..., or any "how many" that does not need the rows themselves. Count the matching rows shows a call.

The result equals read(predicate).count(): same rows, same number. Only the work differs. The read path already classifies the row groups by their filter-pipeline outcome, and count answers two of those outcomes from metadata alone.

items.title: 2. The three routings
items.text:
count() runs the same metadata-only filter pipeline as read(), then routes each row group by its outcome. Two of the four outcomes are answered without decoding a column.

flowchart TD
    pred["count(predicate)"] --> always{"predicate is<br/>ALWAYS_TRUE / ALWAYS_FALSE?"}
    always -->|yes| meta["total row count / 0<br/>(footer metadata)"]
    always -->|no| pipe["run filter pipeline<br/>(metadata only)"]
    pipe --> rg{"per row group<br/>outcome"}
    rg -->|ELIMINATED| zero["+ 0<br/>(pruned, no I/O)"]
    rg -->|MATCHED| rc["+ rowCount<br/>(proven, no decode)"]
    rg -->|FULL / PARTIAL| residual["decode predicate columns only<br/>-> vectorized popcount"]
    zero --> sum["sum"]
    rc --> sum
    residual --> sum
Outcome Contributes Cost ELIMINATED 0 none - the pipeline already proved no row matches MATCHED rowCount() metadata only: statistics proved that all rows match FULL / PARTIAL popcount of the matches decode the predicate columns only, then count columnar

A whole-file ALWAYS_TRUE short-circuits to the summed row counts before the pipeline runs, and ALWAYS_FALSE returns 0. Only the residual FULL / PARTIAL row groups touch column data, and even then only the predicate's columns: never an output projection, never a ParquetRecord.

items.title: 3. Proving a whole row group matches
items.text:
ELIMINATED means that no row matches: it is how the pipeline prunes. MATCHED is its mirror image: all rows match. A proven row group contributes its row count with zero decode.

The proof lives in the STATS tier. StatsEvaluator returns one of four verdicts per row group: Eliminated, PassedAll, Inconclusive (the statistics leave some rows undecided) or NotApplied (no statistics to consult). The pipeline promotes a STATS PassedAll to the MATCHED outcome and skips the later tiers, as it does for Eliminated. For example year > 5 is PassedAll when the row group's min(year) is already above 5.

Because MATCHED makes the read path skip evaluation (count adds the row count, and read() returns the rows without re-testing them), the proof has to be sound, not just useful. A false MATCHED would overcount. The rule boundsCoverEachRow admits a comparison proof only when:

  • nullCount == 0. A null never satisfies a comparison. A column with any null cannot be all-match (year > 5 is false for a null year).
  • the bounds cover each cell: BOOLEAN, INT32 and INT64 always. FLOAT and DOUBLE only when the writer recorded a NaN count of zero: NaN cells lie outside min/max, and under IEEE 754 an ordered comparison never matches them. Binary (BYTE_ARRAY / FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY) is excluded because its statistics may be truncated, leaving the stored max below the true max.

One proof does not go through the bounds. A FLOAT or DOUBLE row group holds nothing but NaN when the writer recorded a NaN count and a null count adding up to its values. With nullCount == 0 each row then matches x = NaN and x <> 1.0, and the row group is MATCHED. NaN bounds alone prove nothing: a writer taking the min and the max over the NaN cells as well records NaN bounds for a row group holding numbers.

Two more conservative edges: a missing null count fails the == 0 test, and an empty row group (rowCount == 0) is never promoted to MATCHED. When in doubt the verdict is Inconclusive or NotApplied, and the row group falls through to the residual count: slower, never wrong.

MATCHED is a shared outcome, not a count-only one. On the read path, a MATCHED row group streams its rows without running the per-row record filter (see The read path).

items.title: 4. Counting the residual: a columnar popcount
items.text:
A FULL or PARTIAL row group is a row group not settled by the statistics. Its rows must be tested. Count does this without building a single record. It decodes the predicate's columns into the usual columnar ParquetRecordBatch, then VectorizedPredicateEvaluator turns the predicate into a BitSet of matching rows. The count is that bitset's cardinality().

  • IsNotNull is a pure popcount over the column's validity mask; IsNull is its complement. No value is compared.
  • A comparison scans the typed primitive array (int[], long[], double[], ...), sets a bit where the comparison holds, and intersects with validity - a null row is structurally excluded, matching the record-level rule.
  • And / Or / Not are BitSet intersection / union / complement of the child masks.

The evaluator is held to the same semantics as the row-by-row RecordLevelEvaluator: both route their comparisons through the shared ValueComparison core (one definition of type coercion and Parquet's unsigned binary ordering). A residual count and a read().count() therefore agree on boundary values. The difference is only the shape of the work - a tight columnar scan and a popcount instead of per-row record assembly.

items.title: 5. What it costs
items.text:
The JMH benchmark CountBenchmark, in internal/parquetry-benchmarks, times count() against a read(predicate).count() baseline. Its file holds 1M rows, with a sorted id column without nulls and 100k rows per row group. It shows three regimes:

  • Proven paths go from O(rows) to O(row groups). When statistics decide the whole file (ALWAYS_TRUE, MATCHED, an IsNotNull on a column without nulls), count decodes no column, and its cost follows the number of row groups. The baseline scans the rows. A layer's feature count is often in this case.
  • The residual path decodes less. It decodes only the predicate columns and counts in columnar form instead of materializing records.
  • ELIMINATED costs the same. read() already drops fully pruned row groups from statistics, and there is no decode to save.

items.title: 6. Edges and limits
items.text:
• Spatial predicates are lowered before counting exactly as they are before reading (covering-column comparisons where the file supports them, or the WKB envelope test where it does not). A bbox count reuses the pruning described in Spatial filtering.
  • Null correctness is identical to the read path: comparisons exclude nulls, IsNull / IsNotNull are decided purely by the validity mask.

items.title: Float statistics
items.text:
In short

Parquetry writes the min/max statistics of float columns in the type-defined order by default, and the readers tested open such files and use the statistics to skip data. Pruning agrees with the per-row comparison on NaN and on the two zeros. IEEE 754 total order is available on request, for files read by readers known to support it.

This page explains how Parquetry writes and reads the min/max statistics of FLOAT, DOUBLE and FLOAT16 columns, what it does with NaN and the two zeros, and when to ask for IEEE 754 total order. It is for developers writing float columns for other readers, and for developers filtering on float columns.

The pruning tiers fed by these statistics are described in The read path.

The guiding rule: the readers tested open the default output and prune it like the files of other writers; IEEE 754 total order is a choice for files with known readers.

items.title: 1. Why float bounds need rules
items.text:
Min and max statistics let a reader skip a row group or a page without decoding it. Two kinds of floating-point values break the plain "smallest and largest value" contract:

  • NaN is unordered: <, <=, >, >= and = are false between NaN and any value, NaN included. Bounds computed over NaN cells hide the numbers of the column, and readers disagree on whether NaN sorts above or below the numbers.
  • -0.0 and +0.0 are equal under IEEE 754 comparison and differ as bit patterns. A minimum of +0.0 hides a -0.0 cell from a reader ordering the two.

The Parquet format answers with a nan_count statistic and with a column order declared per column in the footer. The order tells a reader how the bounds of the column were computed.

items.title: 2. What Parquetry writes
items.text:
Float columns declare the type-defined order by default. A write can ask for IEEE 754 total order instead (section 4). Both orders record a NaN count.

Type-defined order (default) IEEE 754 total order nan_count chunk statistics, page headers, column index the same Bounds of a chunk or page its smallest and largest number; NaN cells are left out the same A zero bound -0.0 as a minimum, +0.0 as a maximum the zero of the cell: -0.0 orders before +0.0 Chunk or page of only NaN no bounds its smallest and largest NaN, sign and payload bits included Chunk with a page of only NaN no column index, as required by the format keeps its column index Deprecated min / max written for FLOAT and DOUBLE the same

A FLOAT or DOUBLE column annotated UNKNOWN keeps the type-defined order in either case.

Dictionary pages keep the bit patterns of NaN cells and of the two zeros: a cell reads back with its sign and payload intact.

items.title: 3. How Parquetry reads them
items.text:
FLOAT and DOUBLE predicates compare as IEEE 754 numbers: <, <=, > and >= never match NaN, and -0.0 equals +0.0. NaN literals are the one extension: x = NaN and IN with a NaN match the NaN cells, and x <> NaN matches the other non-null cells. NOT over a comparison reads as the complementary operator: NOT (x > 5) is x <= 5, and matches no NaN. Pruning has to agree with that row by row. FLOAT16 cells compare as bytes, and their bounds and NaN counts do not prune.

  • Bounds prune comparisons with numbers. A NaN bound is ignored, and a zero bound matches either zero.
  • NaN counts rule on the NaN cells:
  • x = NaN skips a row group or page with a NaN count of zero;
  • a comparison with a number, and x <> NaN, skip a row group or page holding nothing but NaN, known from NaN and null counts adding up to its values;
  • a row group with a NaN count of zero and no null can match a comparison as a whole, and count then answers from metadata.
  • Without NaN counts (files from older writers) NaN cells may sit anywhere: x = NaN prunes nothing, and no float row group matches as a whole.

The rules are the same in both column orders: what is known of NaN cells comes from the counts, never from a NaN bound. Only a total-order column index lists a page of only NaN (section 2), and only such an index lets a read skip that page.

par explain shows these decisions per row group and tier.

items.title: 4. Asking for IEEE 754 total order
items.text:
Total order is the order recommended by the format for float columns: it leaves no ambiguity on NaN and on the zeros, and a chunk with a page of only NaN keeps its column index. The cost is compatibility: the order entered the format in parquet-format 2.13.0 (June 2026), and several readers in use today cannot open a file written in it or do not prune its float columns (section 5).

Choose the order of float statistics shows how to ask for it.

items.title: 5. Reader compatibility
items.text:
This table was measured in October 2026, with the reader versions named in each row. Releases after those versions were not measured. The probe ran on par cp copies of a 1M-row file with float32 columns, NaN cells and one row group of only NaN, against the same queries on the source file written by pyarrow. "Prunes" means the reader skipped the row groups ruled out by a filter on a float column. The probe overwrote the column chunks of those row groups with garbage. A reader that still returned the right rows skipped them. The parquet-java row comes from the Parquetry conformance tests, not from this probe.

Reader Type-defined order (default) IEEE 754 total order Arrow C++ / pyarrow 16 to 24 reads, prunes reads, prunes Arrow C++ / pyarrow 25.0 reads, prunes reads, does not prune float columns arrow-rs / DataFusion 40 to 50 reads, prunes cannot open the file arrow-rs / DataFusion 51 to 54 reads, prunes reads, prunes Polars 1.0 to 1.40 reads cannot open the file Polars 1.44 reads reads DuckDB 0.10 to 1.5 reads, prunes reads, prunes parquet-java 1.18 (conformance tests) reads reads

Notes:

  • GDAL and geopandas read through Arrow C++. Their bbox filters on float32 covering columns were not measured separately.
  • The Polars rows say "reads" alone: Polars 1.30 and later did not skip the row groups of this query on the pyarrow source either. Polars 1.0 and 1.20 skipped them on the default copy as on the source.
  • parquet-java 1.18 is the oracle of the Parquetry conformance tests. For the same cells it writes the same bounds and NaN counts in either order, and the same column indexes in total order. In the type-defined order it writes no column index for a chunk holding a NaN; Parquetry keeps the index unless a page holds only NaN. Its filtered reads of Parquetry files return the same rows with and without pruning.
  • parquet-java 1.17 and earlier ignore the statistics of a column in an order unknown to them, except for a chunk with equal min and max (per its sources; not run here): rows stay correct, with little pruning on those columns.
  • pyarrow 25.0, Polars 1.44, DataFusion 54 and DuckDB 1.5 write the type-defined order for float columns, as read back from a file written by each. parquet-java 1.18 writes total order by default.

items.title: Memory
items.text:
In short

Parquetry reads the memory limit of the container at startup and derives its native memory budgets from the memory left beside the heap. Readers share these budgets, and a pod of another size gets budgets scaled to its own limit. This page describes the budgets, their defaults and how to size them.

This page explains how Parquetry bounds the memory of its reads, and how these bounds relate to a container memory limit. It is for developers and operators running Parquetry in a long-lived server process. The settings are in Tune memory.

The guiding rule: a read is bounded by budgets scaled from the memory left beside the heap by the container, and the native buffers under those budgets leave the process the moment they are freed. The second half holds where the pool maps its buffers, on Linux and macOS with native access allowed (section 3). On malloc, freed memory may stay with the process. The default target is a server process with 1-2 GB for the reader, not "load the file." The fetch and decode stages controlled by these budgets are described in The read path.

items.title: 1. One budget for the process
items.text:
A server such as GeoServer hosts many data stores in one process, and the container holds the process to one memory limit. Parquetry derives its native memory budgets from that limit. This section explains why, and what goes wrong with limits set per store.

Three facts about containers combine into the failure:

  • -Xmx sees the heap only. The JVM heap limit caps the Java heap. Native buffers, thread stacks, metaspace and the memory of native libraries sit outside it.
  • The container limit counts the whole process. The cgroup memory limit counts the heap and the native memory together.
  • The container kills with a signal. When the process crosses the limit, the kernel kills it with SIGKILL. No OutOfMemoryError is thrown, no finally block runs, and the requests in flight get no response.

A store backed by an embedded native engine, reached through JDBC, an Arrow stream or a JNI bridge, keeps most of its working memory outside the heap. Such an engine has limits of its own, such as a cap on its buffer pool and on its threads. Within one engine instance these limits work. The concurrent queries of the instance share the pool, and an overflow becomes a spill to disk or an error returned to the caller, not a kill.

These limits bound one engine instance, and a server runs one instance per store. No setting bounds the sum of the instances, although the container counts that sum. The operator splits the container memory by hand:

sum of the store memory limits + JVM heap + other native memory + spill room <= container memory
sum of the store thread limits                                               <= available cores

A pod of a fixed size can work with this split: the operator computes it once and keeps it current. The split breaks down when one container hosts many stores and a scheduler assigns its memory limit:

  • The split is fixed, and the load moves. Each store needs room for its own peak, although the peaks rarely coincide. The operator either reserves most of the pod for idle stores, or risks a kill when two large scans meet.
  • Stores are added one at a time. A new store changes the sum, and the configuration of one store does not recompute the others.
  • The pod size changes. The split must be recomputed for each pod size. A split computed for a 4 GB pod is too large for a 2 GB pod and wastes most of a 16 GB pod.

A reader decoding in the JVM avoids the split for its heap, because one -Xmx bounds the stores together. Parquetry brings its native buffers under the same rule. At startup it reads the container limit and derives its fetch and decode budgets from the memory left beside the heap (section 2). Readers opened with the default runtime share these budgets. Adding a store adds nothing to tune, and a pod of another size gets budgets scaled to its own limit.

When a budget is full, a read waits for room, then spills its buffers to a memory-mapped file (Native memory and spill). When the disk budget is full too, the read fails with a BudgetExhaustedException. One request fails, and the process keeps serving the others.

items.title: 2. The budgets
items.text:
A read holds memory in three places, and each has its own cap.

Budget Bounds Counted against Default FetchBudget off-heap bytes held by column-chunk fetches, in flight and prefetched the container limit, invisible to -Xmx a fifth of the memory beside the heap off-heap DecodeBudget off-heap bytes held by decoded values kept in native segments the container limit half of the memory beside the heap on-heap DecodeBudget heap bytes held by a read in speculatively decoded batches -Xmx (the JVM heap) 0.25 of Runtime.maxMemory()

"The memory beside the heap" is the container limit minus the maximum heap (ResourceLimits.availableMemoryBytes()). The heap grows to its maximum under load whatever its live set, and the budgets must not count that memory a second time. With the heap at half the container, as -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50 sets it, the fetch cap is a tenth of the container and the off-heap decode cap a quarter. Tune memory replaces the memory figure used to derive the budgets.

The budgets belong to the ParquetRuntime. Readers opened with the default runtime share one set: however many concurrent reads run through it, the totals stay under one cap each. A reader opened with its own runtime gets its own native budgets, and their sum across runtimes is the deployer's to keep inside the container. Tune memory builds a runtime with budgets of its own.

A mandatory fetch buffer, the one for a read's current row group, gets a native segment while the fetch budget has room. When it has none, the fetch waits up to mandatoryBufferWait (1 s by default) for other reads to release room, in first-come order. The read holds no other fetch buffer while it waits, and that is what keeps the wait from deadlocking. When the wait expires, the buffer is a memory-mapped temp file (see native memory and spill), and when the disk budget has no room either, the read fails with a BudgetExhaustedException. A request larger than the whole budget skips the wait and spills at once. A mandatory decode buffer never waits: it is a native segment while the off-heap decode budget has room and a mapped file otherwise. A speculative fetch, for the prefetch window or for decode-ahead, never waits for fetch-budget room and never spills a fetch buffer: it yields while the budget is full, and the row group is fetched when the consumer reaches it. The decoded batches of a row group decoding ahead follow the decode budget's own rule: a batch over that budget spills to disk, or waits for room when spilling is off. The counters behind this are FetchBudget.waitStats() and DiskBudget.stats().

items.title: The caches
items.text:
Beside the budgets of the reads, the process keeps cached data on the heap, in the two pools of the shared tileverse cache manager. The tileverse guide Configure for performance describes the pools, their settings and how the caches key the data of a file.

Parquetry keeps two caches in the metadata pool: the parsed footers (parquetry-footer-metadata) and the page indexes learned from page headers (parquetry-learned-pages, see The read path). A learned page index weighs about 18 bytes a page, plus the bounds of its pages and a fixed 288 bytes. An entry unused for ten minutes expires. An open over an unnamed source never reaches the cache.

The byte-range cache keeps the ranges read from remote storage in the data pool. The GeoTools stores of Parquetry (Parquet, STAC GeoParquet and Iceberg) turn it on by default. par and FileSource.open keep it off. Local files have no byte-range cache.

The metadata of a file is keyed by its name, with the version of the object when the reader knows one, and by its length. Files opened through FileSource have a version, from the listing or the stat lookup that found them. STAC assets, the data files of an Iceberg table and some par commands open their files by key alone. Without a version, a file rewritten under the same name at the same length is served its old entries until they expire. Iceberg never rewrites a data file in place.

The learned cache counts two misses and one load per learned chunk: its hit rate reads low by design. Tune memory sizes the pools, turns the byte-range cache off and clears the caches.

items.title: 3. Where the native memory comes from
items.text:
Off-heap growth is what drives container OOM-kills: it counts against the pod's memory limit but is invisible to -Xmx, and the kernel kills the process before any OutOfMemoryError is thrown. Two things keep Parquetry's native footprint equal to what it holds:

  • The fetch buffers, the decompressed pages and the native decode buffers all come from one SegmentPool. The pool retains returned buffers under byte caps sized to the working set of a loaded server (a fifth of the memory beside the heap for the large class, a tenth for the small one) and frees what sits idle for a minute. A borrow is never refused. The pool's ceiling, equal to what the two native budgets allow in flight, limits retention instead: a returned buffer is kept only while borrowed plus retained bytes stay within it, hence the pool's footprint never exceeds the larger of the ceiling and the bytes in flight. Retention fills what the budgets leave idle instead of adding to them.
  • A pool buffer of 64 KiB or more is an anonymous memory mapping, not a malloc allocation, on Linux and macOS. Memory freed to glibc's malloc does not leave the process: the freed chunk stays parked in the arena of the thread that allocated it, and a server with many threads keeps up to eight arenas per host CPU, each with its own high-water mark. Under concurrent reads, the memory kept that way can exceed the memory in use. A mapping is unmapped when its buffer is freed, and the pages go back to the kernel at once.

The mappings need native access (Allow native access).

items.title: 4. Sizing against a container limit
items.text:
Peak process memory is approximately:

maxHeap (-Xmx; the heap grows to it under load)
  + the pool's memory, in flight and retained (at most FetchBudget + off-heap DecodeBudget)
  + decompressed pages (one per projected column of each row group being decoded)
  + JVM native baseline (metaspace, code cache, GC structures, thread stacks)

The pool's ceiling is the two budgets' total, and what the pool retains between bursts counts inside it, not on top. The decompressed pages are borrowed from the pool without a budget reservation: a read decoding n row groups ahead holds up to n pages per projected column, each the file's page size, usually about a megabyte. With -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50 the first term is half the container and the pool takes at most 35% of it before fetches queue for room and then spill to disk. About 15% is left for the pages, the JVM baseline and the page cache.

The on-heap DecodeBudget and the caches are inside -Xmx, and add nothing to the formula. The budgets bound speculative work and native buffers, not the heap of the mandatory current row group: a read unable to fit the working set of one row group inside -Xmx fails with an OutOfMemoryError. Size the container lists the sizing rules and the JVM settings beside Parquetry's own.

items.text:
Paths are relative to the io/tileverse/parquetry package of its module. The io/ files are in parquetry-io, the geotools/ file in parquetry-geotools, and the others in parquetry-core.
