items.title: Spatial filtering
items.text:
In short

A bounding box filter compares the bounding box of each geometry with the query box, and its result is exact for that comparison. Parquetry skips row groups and pages with the bbox covering columns of a file, and row groups with its GeoParquet 2.0 bounds, then tests the remaining rows. An exact geometry test, such as a true intersection, runs on the rows left by that pruning.

This page explains how a spatial predicate on a GeoParquet geometry column turns into pruned row groups, skipped pages and an exact per-row test. It is for developers filtering GeoParquet by location, and for operators who want to know which files prune well.

Spatial filtering is part of the read path: read The read path first for the four stages of a read.

The guiding rule: the bbox relations compare the 2D bounding box of the geometry only. They are rectangle relations, evaluated exactly. A true geometry test, such as a real intersects against the curve and not its envelope, goes through a geometry engine behind the GeometryFilter<T> SPI (section 6).

items.title: 1. The predicate family
items.text:
The predicate ADT exposes a closed family of four bbox relations under the sealed Predicate.Spatial. Each compares the geometry's 2D bounding box against a query Bbox, edges inclusive, Z ignored.

Relation True when the geometry's bbox ... Builder BboxIntersects overlaps the query box Pred.col("geometry").bboxIntersects(q) BboxContains encloses the query box Pred.col("geometry").bboxContains(q) BboxCoveredBy is enclosed by the query box Pred.col("geometry").bboxCoveredBy(q) BboxEquals matches the query box on all four edges Pred.col("geometry").bboxEquals(q)

The query box is a Bbox: Bbox.of2d(minX, minY, maxX, maxY) (or of3d(...), though the relations compare X/Y only). The family is closed on purpose: each relation in it has an exact evaluation. There are no DWithin, Within or Overlaps stubs returning wrong rows.

items.title: 2. Using it
items.text:
A spatial read is an ordinary read() with a spatial predicate. The geometry column is decoded for the filter even when it is outside the projection. Filter by location shows such a read.

A spatial predicate composes with the rest of the ADT: And / Or with attribute predicates, and Not around a spatial relation, behave as usual (see section 5 for the one subtlety, null geometries).

items.title: 3. How it filters
items.text:
A spatial predicate is filtered at three levels, cheapest first, in the same "filter, then fetch, then decode" order as other predicates. The statistics present in the file decide which row-group and page levels apply (section 4).

flowchart TD
    pred["Predicate.Spatial leaf"] --> covering{"file has bbox.*<br/>covering columns?"}

    covering -->|yes| lower["lower to numeric comparisons<br/>SpatialCoveringRewrite"]
    lower --> tiers["STATS + COLUMN_INDEX tiers<br/>prune row groups AND pages"]
    tiers --> recordCmp["record level: covering comparisons,<br/>then WkbEnvelope.matches on the<br/>surviving rows"]

    covering -->|no| native["SPATIAL tier<br/>SpatialBoundsEvaluator"]
    native --> rg["eliminate row groups whose native<br/>per-row-group geometry bbox is disjoint"]
    rg --> recordWkb["record level: WkbEnvelope.matches<br/>(short-circuiting WKB walk)"]

Record level - the exact test. WkbEnvelope.matches walks the geometry's WKB and decides the relation while it reads, stopping as soon as the answer is fixed: BboxIntersects / BboxContains return true the moment the running envelope satisfies the relation; BboxCoveredBy returns false on the first vertex outside the query; BboxEquals needs the full envelope. The walk is shared with the write-side statistics accumulator; one WKB parser serves both sides.

The walk accepts both WKB type-code encodings: ISO (Z/M/ZM via the +1000/+2000/+3000 offsets) and EWKB (Z/M via the 0x80000000/0x40000000 high-bit flags, as JTS and PostGIS write them). An EWKB 0x20000000 SRID flag is recognized and its 4-byte payload skipped. Per the parquet-format spec, the geospatial_types recorded in the written statistics are always normalized to ISO codes, whatever the encoding of the input.

Row-group and page pruning comes from one of two mechanisms:

  • Covering-column lowering. A GeoParquet file with a bbox covering (1.1 or 2.0) stores a box enclosing each row's geometry in four bbox.* sidecar columns. GeoParquet allows that box to be wider than the geometry's own bounding box, and Parquetry's FLOAT covering rounds its bounds outward. A relation lowers to the comparisons on those columns satisfied by the matching rows, a necessary condition rather than an equivalent. BboxIntersects(q) and BboxCoveredBy(q) lower to an overlap test, xmin <= q.maxX AND xmax >= q.minX AND ymin <= q.maxY AND ymax >= q.minY. BboxContains(q) and BboxEquals(q) lower to a test that the covering encloses the query box. SpatialCoveringRewrite adds that conjunction beside the spatial leaf at read time, and the existing STATS and COLUMN_INDEX tiers prune row groups and pages from the sidecar columns' statistics. Page pruning needs a column index on those columns, or pages learned from their page headers by an earlier read (Without a page index). The spatial leaf stays in the predicate and decides the surviving rows from their geometry WKB. That test keeps the answer exact.
  • Native row-group bounds. A GeoParquet 2.0 file stores a per-row-group geometry bounding box in the column chunk's statistics. The SPATIAL tier (SpatialBoundsEvaluator) eliminates a row group whose box is disjoint from the query (BboxContains instead keeps only groups whose box can enclose the query). This is row-group granularity only - native statistics are per chunk, not per page.

items.title: 4. Which path applies
items.text:
The two pruning mechanisms target different files, and a single read picks the mechanism supported by the file:

The file has ... Row-group pruning Page pruning Record-level test bbox.* covering columns (GeoParquet 1.1 or 2.0) yes (lowered comparisons) yes, with a column index or learned pages covering comparisons, then WkbEnvelope.matches on the WKB native per-row-group geometry stats only (GeoParquet 2.0) yes (SPATIAL tier) no WkbEnvelope.matches on WKB neither no no WkbEnvelope.matches on WKB

A file with a covering takes the lowering path, whatever the GeoParquet version declared in its geo document. It prunes pages too, from the first read when its covering columns have a column index. Without one, pruning starts at the second read of a row group, when that read scans only learned columns. A GeoParquet 2.0 file without a covering takes the native path, at row-group granularity. With no usable statistics, nothing is pruned and the result is still exact: the record-level test decides the rows.

Parquetry's writer emits both by default: native per-row-group geometry statistics and a bbox covering. Write a GeoParquet file lists the options.

Pruning is conservative everywhere: a row group or page is dropped only when its statistics prove no row in it can match; pruning never changes which rows a read returns, only how much work it does. Spatial clustering is what makes it pay off; a file whose geometries are spread evenly across row groups prunes little.

items.title: 5. Null geometries
items.text:
A null (absent) geometry has no bounding box and therefore no spatial truth value. Under OGC simple-feature semantics a relation against it is unknown, and a WHERE keeps a row only when the predicate is true. A null-geometry row is excluded from a spatial predicate and from its negation - the same way col = v and col <> v both exclude a null col:

geometry bboxIntersects(q) NOT bboxIntersects(q) present, overlaps kept dropped present, disjoint dropped kept null dropped dropped

A predicate and its negation are not complementary when nulls are present; the null rows fall out of both. This only matters for an optional geometry column - a required geometry never triggers it.

items.title: 6. The bbox-only contract
items.text:
The four relations compare bounding boxes, not geometries. For a polygon query they answer "could these interact?", not "do these shapes actually intersect?". That coarse answer is exactly what a spatial index gives, and it is enough to prune the read down to a small candidate set.

True-geometry filtering, such as a real intersection against the curve, needs a geometry engine. The materializer decoding WKB into a geometry object is output-only, and it never runs in the filter path.

The exact test runs either in the consumer, on the candidates returned by a bbox relation, or inside the read, as a GeometryFilter<T> (filter/GeometryFilter.java). A geometry filter provides a sound bbox lowering for coarse pruning plus an exact matches test. The reader prunes with the lowering, then runs the exact test per surviving row, dropping non-matches before their other columns materialize. parquetry-core ships JtsGeometryFilter (package io.tileverse.parquetry.geo) over the JTS topology predicates. A geometry filter in the read decodes each surviving geometry once for the test, and output materialization decodes the WKB again. Apply an exact geometry test shows both ways.

items.title: 7. Where to look
items.text:
Paths are relative to the io/tileverse/parquetry package of parquetry-core.

Concern Start in Predicate family + builders filter/Predicate.java (Predicate.Spatial), filter/Pred.java Query box + 2D relations filter/Bbox.java Shared WKB walk + exact match internal/filter/spatial/WkbEnvelope.java Record-level evaluation internal/filter/RecordLevelEvaluator.java Covering-column lowering internal/filter/spatial/SpatialCoveringRewrite.java Native row-group pruning internal/filter/SpatialBoundsEvaluator.java, filter/explain/Tier.java, internal/filter/spatial/SpatialBoundsSource.java Exact geometry gate (SPI) filter/GeometryFilter.java, Predicate.geometryFilter(...) JTS-backed exact filter geo/JtsGeometryFilter.java Benchmarks internal/parquetry-benchmarks/.../SpatialPruningBenchmark.java, SpatialGateBenchmark.java, JtsSpatialFilterBenchmark.java

Scope: bbox-based spatial filtering over a GeoParquet geometry column. True geometry materialization (WKB to a JTS geometry) is in parquetry-core, in the io.tileverse.parquetry.geo package. The general read path is in The read path.

items.title: Developer guide
items.text:
You want to build Parquetry from its sources, try a change, or contribute one. This section is for you. To use Parquetry in an application, start with Getting started instead.

  • Architecture shows the modules, their main classes and the path of a read, as C4 diagrams.
  • Build from source clones the repository with its test files, builds the modules, runs the tests and builds this site.
  • Releases explains how versions reach Maven Central, and how this site is published.
  • Contribute lists the conventions followed by a change: formatting, test names, commit messages and license headers.

The source code is on GitHub, under the Apache License 2.0.

items.title: Architecture
items.text:
This page shows how Parquetry is built, in seven C4 diagrams, from the systems around it down to the classes of a read. It is for developers who read or change the code. The diagrams name real modules and types: open a type in the source to see the details. Select a diagram to open it at full size.

The diagrams are generated from a Structurizr model kept in the repository, under docs/structurizr/. In the diagrams, brown boxes are parts of Parquetry, grey boxes are other systems, and lighter brown boxes with a dashed border are experimental modules.

items.title: System context
items.text: Parquetry is a set of Java libraries, used by Java applications and by GeoServer. GeoServer and GeoServer Cloud reach Parquetry through its GeoTools data store. Parquetry does not talk to object storage itself: it reads byte ranges, lists files and writes files through tileverse-storage. A read can also be handed as Apache Arrow to an analytics engine.

items.title: Containers
items.text: The containers are the Maven modules of Parquetry, and the arrows are the dependencies declared in their POMs. parquetry-core reads and writes single files, over three foundation modules: parquetry-io, parquetry-format and parquetry-compression. parquetry-catalog reads many files as one dataset, and the integration modules build on it. parquetry-io holds the adapter to tileverse-storage. parquetry-core, the Iceberg, STAC and GeoTools modules and par also use tileverse-storage types directly, and the diagram leaves those arrows out to stay readable. Modules lists the modules with their status.

items.title: Components of parquetry-core
items.text: The diagram shows the read pipeline and the writer of one file. ParquetFileReader opens a file and decodes its footer once. ReadPlanner runs the filter pipeline of a query on the metadata of the file. FilterPipeline runs one class per tier: STATS, SPATIAL, COLUMN_INDEX and BLOOM_FILTER. The fifth tier, RECORD_LEVEL, runs later, during the decode, in VectorizedPredicateEvaluator. The fetch classes read the byte ranges of the surviving row groups through parquetry-io. The decode classes turn their pages into batches. BatchPipeline hands the batches, or records built by a Materializer, to the caller. ParquetFileWriter writes row groups, the page index, the bloom filters and the footer. The read path explains the same classes step by step.

items.title: Components of parquetry-catalog
items.text: A DatasetCatalog gives access to datasets by name. FilesetCatalog is the catalog over a listing of files: it builds one dataset merging the files, or one dataset per file. It reads the footers of the files on virtual threads, and parses Hive partition directories such as year=2024/. A FilesetDataset prunes its files before a query, then reads the surviving files several at a time. It reads a file through a ParquetSource, over the reader of parquetry-core. The Iceberg and STAC modules provide their own catalogs and datasets behind the same two interfaces. Multi-file datasets shows how to use them.

items.title: Components of parquetry-geotools
items.text: GeoServer opens the store through GeoParquetDataStoreFactory. The factory lists the files and opens a FilesetCatalog over them. CatalogDataStore publishes one feature type per dataset, and CatalogFeatureSource serves the features, the count and the bounds of one of them. QueryTranslator and FilterToPredicate turn a GeoTools query into a predicate, the columns to decode, and the filter left to GeoTools. DatasetFeatureReader builds the features from the rows of the read. ScreenMapReadProbe passes the pixels already drawn on a map to the read. GeoParquetExporter writes features as a GeoParquet file. The GeoTools data store describes the store from the user side.

items.title: A filtered read
items.text: The numbers give the order of the calls in one filtered read of a file. Steps 1 to 11 run inside the read call: the filter pipeline prunes the row groups and pages on the metadata, and the read returns a lazy stream. Steps 12 to 20 run when the caller pulls the first rows. The decode asks for the bytes of a row group, the fetch reads the byte ranges of its surviving pages from storage, and the masked scan evaluates the predicate while it decodes. The read path follows the same steps in more detail.

items.title: A GeoServer request
items.text: A WMS GetMap or a WFS GetFeature request asks the store for the features of a layer. The feature source translates the filter of the request into a predicate, and opens a reader with it. For a map, it also passes the drawn pixels to the read. The dataset of parquetry-catalog prunes its files and reads the surviving ones with parquetry-core. The reads fetch only the byte ranges left after filtering, through tileverse-storage. GeoServer then iterates over the features, one per matching row.

items.title: Build from source
items.text: You want to build Parquetry from its sources and run its tests, to try a change or to use a version not released yet. This page clones the repository, builds the modules, runs the tests and builds this documentation site.

items.title: Requirements
items.text:
• JDK 25. The build compiles with Java 25 preview features.
  • Git.
  • Docker, for part of the integration tests. These tests start object storage emulators in containers, and are skipped when Docker is not available.

Build with ./mvnw, the Maven wrapper at the root of the repository. It downloads the Maven version used by the project, and reads the JVM options of the build from .mvn/jvm.config.

items.title: Clone with the test files
items.text:
The tests read files from other repositories: the Apache Parquet test corpus (apache/parquet-testing) and the GeoParquet examples and test data (opengeospatial/geoparquet, geoparquet/geoparquet-testing). These repositories are Git submodules under internal/parquetry-testkit. Clone with them, or the conformance tests cannot run:

git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/tileverse-io/parquetry.git

In a clone made without them, fetch them:

git submodule update --init --recursive

items.title: Build and test
items.text:
# Compile and run the unit tests
./mvnw test

# Unit and integration tests
./mvnw verify

# Package the modules without running the tests
./mvnw package -DskipTests

Unit tests are the classes named *Test, and run in the test phase. Integration tests are the classes named *IT, and run in the verify phase. They read the test corpora, compare the results with other Parquet readers, and read files through the storage emulators.

items.title: Build one module
items.text:
Select a module by its artifact id, and add -am to also build the modules it depends on:

./mvnw -pl :parquetry-core -am test

Without -am, Maven takes the other modules from your local repository, where they may be older than your sources, or missing. Modules lists the artifact ids.

Pass JVM options to the test JVMs through extraArgLine, for example a larger heap:

./mvnw -pl :parquetry-core -am verify -DextraArgLine="-Xmx2g"

items.title: Format the code
items.text:
The build formats the Java sources and the POM files with Spotless. To format without building:

./mvnw spotless:apply

Contribute describes the formatting rules.

items.title: Measure test coverage
items.text:
./mvnw -Pcoverage verify

The build writes a coverage report of all modules to internal/parquetry-coverage-report/target/site/jacoco-aggregate/index.html.

items.title: Build this site
items.text:
The sources of this site are under docs/. The build needs Python 3.11 or newer, and Docker for the architecture diagrams:

# Create the Python environment, generate the diagrams, build the site into docs/site/
./docs/build.sh

# Serve the site at http://127.0.0.1:8000, reloading on changes
./docs/serve.sh

The build is strict: a link to a missing page or anchor fails it. The README of the docs directory describes the layout of the sources and how to add a page.

items.title: Contribute
items.text: You want to fix a bug or add a feature to Parquetry. This page lists the conventions followed by a change. Build from source sets up the build first.

items.title: Formatting
items.text: Spotless formats the code with palantir-java-format, and sorts the elements of the POM files. A build formats the sources in its validate phase, before it compiles them. ./mvnw spotless:apply formats them without building. Build before you commit, and commit the formatted files.

items.title: License headers
items.text: Each Java file starts with the Apache License 2.0 header used by the project. Spotless adds it to a new file during the build.

items.title: Tests
items.text:
The name of a test class decides when it runs:

  • A class named *Test holds unit tests, run by ./mvnw test.
  • A class named *IT holds integration tests, run by ./mvnw verify.

Tests use JUnit Jupiter and AssertJ.

items.title: Commit messages
items.text:
The title of a commit follows Conventional Commits: a type, an optional scope, and a short description.

Type For feat A new capability fix A bug fix perf A performance improvement refactor A change of structure, with the same behavior test Tests only docs Documentation only chore Build and maintenance

For example: fix: wrong rows from filters when the offset index misplaces pages, or feat(geotools): cache remote byte ranges by default.

items.title: Use of AI tools
items.text: Contributions written with the help of AI tools follow the Tileverse policy, published at tileverse.io/ai.

items.title: Releases
items.text: You want to know how a Parquetry version reaches Maven Central, or how to use a build of main before it is released. GitHub Actions workflows build, test and publish each version, and publish this site.

items.title: Pull request checks
items.text:
Pull requests and pushes to main run the same checks:

  • Lint: make lint runs the formatting step of the build, with Spotless.
  • Build: ./mvnw verify on Linux, macOS and Windows, with Java 25. The Linux build also measures test coverage.

The checks skip changes that touch only docs/ or Markdown files.

items.title: Snapshots
items.text:
A push to main publishes the build as a -SNAPSHOT version to the snapshot repository of Maven Central, https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots/. To use a snapshot, declare that repository in your build with snapshots enabled.

The publishing workflow skips the tests and does not wait for the pull request checks. A push touching only docs/ or Markdown files publishes no snapshot, and neither does a commit whose message contains [skip-publish].

items.title: Releases
items.text:
Pushing a tag whose name starts with a digit, such as 1.0.0 or 2.0-RC1, publishes a release. The workflow builds and tests the tagged commit, publishes that exact version to Maven Central, then creates the matching GitHub release. The tag name is the version. A tag starting with another character publishes nothing.

A maintainer can also release any commit with any version by hand, from the same workflow.

The project version in the POM files is ${revision}. The release workflow sets it from the tag. Other builds use the -SNAPSHOT version of main.

items.title: This site
items.text:
A separate workflow builds the site from docs/ when a change touches that directory:

  • On a pull request, it builds the site to check it. A link to a missing page or anchor fails the build.
  • On a push to main, it builds the site and publishes it to parquetry.io.

The site follows main. It may describe features newer than the latest release; Getting started names the release.

The README of the workflows directory describes each workflow in detail.

items.title: Experimental parts
items.text:
Experimental

The parts listed here work, but their API, options and behavior may change between releases.

Parquetry reads Apache Iceberg tables and STAC GeoParquet collections, and has a command line tool, par. These parts work and have tests, but they are labeled experimental. This page says what the label means.

items.title: What experimental means
items.text:
Parquetry has not reached 1.0, and its API may still change before then. The experimental parts change more freely than the others:

  • Their Java API, their options and their output may change between releases.
  • Their pages list known gaps. A gap may close, or the behavior around it may change.

The stable parts are listed on the home page.

items.title: The experimental parts
items.text:
• Apache Iceberg tables: parquetry-iceberg reads a table, or a warehouse of tables, as datasets.
  • STAC GeoParquet collections: parquetry-stac reads the collections of a STAC catalog as datasets.
  • The par command line tool inspects, filters and copies files.

items.title: In GeoTools and GeoServer
items.text:
The GeoTools module of Parquetry registers a STAC GeoParquet store and an Iceberg store next to the "Parquet" store (The other stores of the module). A system property set to true hides a store: parquetry.geotools.stac-geoparquet.disabled or parquetry.geotools.iceberg.disabled.

GeoServer Cloud ships both stores disabled: it sets the two properties to true at startup, unless they are already set. Start the JVM with -Dparquetry.geotools.iceberg.disabled=false, or -Dparquetry.geotools.stac-geoparquet.disabled=false, to turn one on (GeoServer Cloud).

items.title: Apache Iceberg tables
items.text:
Experimental

parquetry-iceberg and its GeoTools store work, but their API, options and behavior may change between releases.

You have an Apache Iceberg table on a file system or in object storage, and want to read it from Java or publish it in GeoServer, without the Iceberg and Hadoop libraries. parquetry-iceberg reads the table as one dataset: one count, one stream of rows, and the data files unable to match the filter left unopened. An Iceberg table is a set of Parquet data files, listed by metadata files: a metadata.json document names the snapshots of the table, and manifest files list the data files of a snapshot.

It needs parquetry-iceberg, with the BOM imported as in Getting started:

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.tileverse.parquetry</groupId>
  <artifactId>parquetry-iceberg</artifactId>
</dependency>

Like parquetry-catalog, it uses Java 25 preview features: start the JVM with --enable-preview (Getting started).

items.title: Read a table
items.text:
The directory orders holds a table partitioned by category: the partitions a, b and c hold 100 rows each, with an id and an amount column. The program counts the rows, prints the first three ids of category b, and shows which data files the filter skips:

import static io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Pred.col;

import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ReadOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.dataset.ParquetDataset;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.dataset.explain.DatasetExplainPlan;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Projection;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.iceberg.IcebergOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.iceberg.IcebergTableCatalog;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.record.ParquetRecord;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ColumnPath;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class ReadIcebergTable {

    private static final ColumnPath ID = ColumnPath.of("id");

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Path tableDir = Path.of("orders");
        Predicate filter = col("category").eq("b");

        try (IcebergTableCatalog catalog = IcebergTableCatalog.openLocal(tableDir, IcebergOptions.defaults())) {
            String name = catalog.datasets().getFirst();
            ParquetDataset table = catalog.dataset(name);
            long total = table.count(Predicate.ALWAYS_TRUE, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS);
            long matching = table.count(filter, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS);
            System.out.println(name + ": " + total + " rows, " + matching + " in category b");

            try (Stream<ParquetRecord> rows = table.read(filter, Projection.ALL, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS)) {
                rows.limit(3).forEach(row -> System.out.println(row.getLong(ID)));
            }

            DatasetExplainPlan plan = table.explain(filter, Projection.ALL, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS);
            System.out.println(plan.toAsciiTable());
        }
    }
}

It prints, with the plan cut after its list of files:

orders: 300 rows, 100 in category b
1000
1001
1002
predicate: Eq[col=ColumnPath[dot=category], v=StringVal[value=b]]
1 kept, 2 skipped  (200 rows pruned without opening a file)

location                                 outcome         rows   reason
file:///iceberg-partitioned/by_category/data/category=a/00000-0-1f83630d-08c1-4462-a8ca-10b98714a70a.parquet SKIP             100   Eq category: value outside [min, max]
file:///iceberg-partitioned/by_category/data/category=b/00000-1-1f83630d-08c1-4462-a8ca-10b98714a70a.parquet KEEP             100   kept
file:///iceberg-partitioned/by_category/data/category=c/00000-2-1f83630d-08c1-4462-a8ca-10b98714a70a.parquet SKIP             100   Eq category: value outside [min, max]
  • IcebergTableCatalog.openLocal finds the current metadata.json of the table: the version named by metadata/version-hint.text, or else the highest vN.metadata.json. It reads the current snapshot and its manifests.
  • The catalog holds one dataset, named after the directory. The dataset has the read methods of Multi-file datasets: read, readBatches, count, bounds and explain.
  • The locations in the plan are the ones recorded in the metadata of the table, when it was written.
  • The read skips a data file when the column bounds of its manifest entry, or its partition value, rule it out. It never opens such a file. In a kept file, the read skips row groups and pages as in a single file.
  • Closing the catalog closes the data files.

The par command line tool reads a table directory the same way: par head orders prints its first rows (The par command line tool).

items.title: Pick a snapshot or a metadata file
items.text:
IcebergOptions.defaults() reads the current snapshot. The builder pins another one, or a metadata document:

IcebergOptions snapshot = IcebergOptions.builder().snapshotId(7189951345053510387L).build();
IcebergOptions metadata = IcebergOptions.builder()
        .metadataLocation(tableLocation + "/metadata/v3.metadata.json")
        .build();

items.title: Read from object storage
items.text:
IcebergTableCatalog.openStorage reads a table through a tileverse Storage rooted at the table, with the backends of Cloud storage:

import io.tileverse.storage.Storage;
import io.tileverse.storage.StorageFactory;
import java.net.URI;
import java.util.Properties;

URI location = URI.create("s3://my-bucket/warehouse/sales/orders");
Storage storage = StorageFactory.open(location, new Properties());
try (IcebergTableCatalog catalog =
        IcebergTableCatalog.openStorage(location.toString(), storage, IcebergOptions.defaults())) {
    ParquetDataset table = catalog.dataset(catalog.datasets().getFirst());
}

The catalog takes ownership of the storage, and closes it with itself. An HTTP server cannot list the metadata directory: for a table served over HTTP, pin the metadata document with metadataLocation.

items.title: Read a warehouse of tables
items.text:
IcebergWarehouseCatalog reads a directory of tables as one catalog, with one dataset per table:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.iceberg.IcebergWarehouseCatalog;

try (IcebergWarehouseCatalog warehouse = IcebergWarehouseCatalog.openLocal(Path.of("warehouse"))) {
    for (String name : warehouse.datasets()) {
        ParquetDataset table = warehouse.dataset(name);
    }
}

The catalog finds the tables below the directory, as <namespace...>/<table>/metadata/*.metadata.json, and names the tables after their paths: warehouse/sales/orders becomes the dataset sales.orders. A table opens on its first use, at its current snapshot. IcebergWarehouseCatalog.open(location, storage) reads a warehouse in object storage. For a store unable to list directories, ofLocalTables and ofTables take the names and locations of the tables instead.

items.title: What it reads
items.text:
• Iceberg format versions 1, 2 and 3.
  • Copy-on-write and merge-on-read tables. Position deletes, equality deletes and deletion vectors apply during the scan, and a deleted row is never returned.
  • The current schema of the table, over data files written with older schemas: renamed, added, dropped and reordered top-level columns. An added column reads as null, or as its initial-default value. Limits lists the exceptions.
  • Type promotions: int to long, float to double, and a wider decimal precision.
  • Data files without field ids, through the schema.name-mapping.default property of the table.
  • The primitive types, decimal, uuid, fixed and the nanosecond timestamps included. The geometry and geography types of format version 3 read as WKB geometries, with the coordinate reference system declared in the type.
  • The row lineage columns of format version 3, _row_id and _last_updated_sequence_number, when a projection names them.
  • Partitioned tables. The value of an identity partition fills its column, also when the data files leave that column out.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• The module reads tables. It does not write them.
  • A table is found by its location. The module has no client for the Iceberg REST catalog or other catalog services.
  • A read uses the current snapshot, or one pinned by its id. Branches, tags and timestamps do not select a snapshot.
  • Only identity partitions skip files by their partition value. A filter on the source column of a day, bucket or truncate partition skips files by the column bounds of the manifests, not by the partition value.
  • Nested columns are matched by name. A data file whose nested field ids disagree with the table, as after the rename of a nested field, fails with an error rather than return wrong values.
  • An added geometry or geography column cannot read as null. A read of a data file written before the column was added fails with an error.
  • A table with an initial-default on a struct, list or map column, or on a nanosecond timestamp column, fails to open.

items.title: In GeoTools and GeoServer
items.text: The GeoTools store selected by the iceberg parameter opens a table directory, or a warehouse with one feature type per table, locally or in object storage. Its fid parameter names the column of the feature ids, and the storage.* parameters configure the backend as for the "Parquet" store. GeoServer Cloud ships this store disabled (Experimental parts).

items.title: STAC GeoParquet collections
items.text:
Experimental

parquetry-stac and its GeoTools store work, but their API, options and behavior may change between releases.

You have a STAC catalog whose items point at GeoParquet files, and want to query a collection as one table from Java or publish it in GeoServer. parquetry-stac reads the collections of the catalog as datasets, one per collection, and skips the files of the items outside a spatial filter without opening them. A STAC catalog (SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog) is a tree of JSON documents: a catalog links to collections, a collection links to items, and an item has a bounding box and assets, the links to its files.

It needs parquetry-stac, with the BOM imported as in Getting started:

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.tileverse.parquetry</groupId>
  <artifactId>parquetry-stac</artifactId>
</dependency>

Like parquetry-catalog, it uses Java 25 preview features: start the JVM with --enable-preview (Getting started).

items.title: Read a collection
items.text:
The catalog catalog.json has one collection, building, with two items. The item item-west has the bounding box [0, 0, 10, 10] and points at building/parts/west.parquet. The item item-east has the bounding box [100, 0, 110, 10] and points at building/parts/east.parquet. Each file holds two points. The program counts the points of the collection inside a box around the east item, and prints the plan of the read:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ReadOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.dataset.ParquetDataset;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.dataset.explain.DatasetExplainPlan;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Bbox;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Projection;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ColumnPath;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.stac.ContainerStorages;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.stac.StacCatalogOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.stac.StacDatasetCatalog;
import io.tileverse.stac.JsonStacReader;
import java.net.URI;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.Properties;

public class ReadStacCollection {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        URI catalogUri = Path.of("catalog.json").toAbsolutePath().toUri();
        Bbox window = Bbox.of2d(95, -5, 115, 15);
        Predicate filter = new Predicate.Spatial.BboxIntersects(ColumnPath.of("geometry"), window);

        try (ContainerStorages storages = new ContainerStorages(new Properties());
                StacDatasetCatalog catalog = StacDatasetCatalog.open(
                        catalogUri, storages, new JsonStacReader(), StacCatalogOptions.defaults())) {
            System.out.println("collections: " + catalog.datasets());
            ParquetDataset buildings = catalog.dataset("building");
            long matching = buildings.count(filter, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS);
            System.out.println(matching + " matching rows");

            DatasetExplainPlan plan = buildings.explain(filter, Projection.ALL, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS);
            System.out.println(plan.toAsciiTable());
        }
    }
}

It prints, with the plan cut after its summary:

collections: [building]
2 matching rows
predicate: BboxIntersects[col=ColumnPath[dot=geometry], bbox=Bbox[minX=95.0, minY=-5.0, maxX=115.0, maxY=15.0, minZ=0.0, maxZ=0.0, is3d=false]]
1 kept, 1 skipped

The list of files in the plan shows west.parquet skipped, with the reason geometry row-group bbox excludes the query, and east.parquet kept.

  • StacDatasetCatalog.open reads the catalog and collection documents, and stops there. The item documents are read when a query needs them, and a GeoParquet file is opened on its first read.
  • The catalog has one dataset per collection, named after the collection id. The dataset has the read methods of Multi-file datasets: read, readBatches, count, bounds and explain.
  • The bounding box of an item becomes the bounds of its file. A file whose item box lies outside a spatial filter is skipped before its footer is read. In a kept file, the read skips row groups and pages as in a single file.
  • ContainerStorages opens one tileverse Storage per directory of documents or files, with the backend selected by its URI. A catalog served over HTTP can point at files in S3. The Properties give the credentials and settings of the backends (Cloud storage).
  • Closing the catalog closes the files and the storages.

items.title: Read a stac-geoparquet table of items
items.text:
A stac-geoparquet file stores STAC items as the rows of a Parquet file. GeoParquetStacReader reads such a file as the index of a catalog, in place of the JSON documents:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.stac.GeoParquetStacReader;

URI items = URI.create("s3://my-bucket/stac/items.parquet");
try (ContainerStorages storages = new ContainerStorages(new Properties());
        StacDatasetCatalog catalog = StacDatasetCatalog.open(
                items, storages, new GeoParquetStacReader(), StacCatalogOptions.defaults())) {
    System.out.println(catalog.datasets());
}

The reader takes the id, bbox, assets, collection and datetime columns of the items, and leaves the geometry and the property columns undecoded. The stac-geoparquet metadata in the footer of the file declares the collections. A collection named in the collection column but not declared gets its extent from the bounding boxes of its items.

items.title: Options
items.text:
StacCatalogOptions.builder() sets two options:

  • parquetMediaTypes sets the media types of the assets read as GeoParquet files. The default is application/vnd.apache.parquet, application/x-parquet and application/parquet. An asset without a media type counts when its link ends in .parquet.
  • geometryColumn names the geometry column of the collections, geometry by default. The bounding box of an item skips its file under a filter on that column.

items.title: What it reads
items.text:
• A static catalog of JSON documents, local or remote, or a stac-geoparquet table of items.
  • A catalog with a latest property naming one of its child catalogs: only that child is read, as in a catalog of releases.
  • Item bounding boxes in 2D or 3D. A 3D box skips files by its X and Y ranges.
  • Items without a bounding box, or with a box in an unknown shape. Their files are always kept.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
• The module reads catalogs. It does not write them.
  • It has no client for the STAC API, the search service of dynamic catalogs. It reads static catalogs and item tables.
  • A stac-geoparquet table serves as an index of items with external files. Its own rows are not read as features.
  • The datetime of the items does not skip files.
  • A collection without GeoParquet assets is listed with the others. Reading it fails with an error naming the collection.

items.title: In GeoTools and GeoServer
items.text: The GeoTools store selected by the stac-geoparquet parameter opens a catalog, with one feature type per collection. The parameter takes the URI of a catalog.json, of a directory holding one (the URI ends in /), or of a stac-geoparquet .parquet file. The storage.* parameters configure the backends as for the "Parquet" store, without storage.provider: the backend follows the URIs of the documents and files. GeoServer Cloud ships this store disabled (Experimental parts).

items.title: GeoTools and GeoServer
items.text: You run GeoServer or GeoServer Cloud and want to publish GeoParquet files as map layers, or you build a service on GeoTools and want to read them. Parquetry provides a GeoTools data store for both. GeoServer Cloud 3.1.0 and newer include it and enable it by default.

items.title: Pick your setup
items.text:
• GeoServer Cloud

    Publish GeoParquet files as layers through the REST API, and download any vector layer as GeoParquet or Arrow IPC through WFS.

    GeoServer Cloud

  • GeoServer

    Install the plugin, then create a "Parquet" store from the web interface and publish its layers.

    The GeoServer plugin

  • A GeoTools application

    Open the store with DataStoreFinder and query its feature sources from Java.

    The GeoTools data store

  • Pods in Kubernetes

    Choose the CPU and memory of a pod serving Parquetry layers.

    Size a GeoServer pod

items.title: What a layer gets
items.text:
A layer served by the Parquetry store reads its files from a local volume, an HTTP server, Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage. A file, a directory of files or a tree of Hive partitions can be one layer, and a directory can also give one layer per file.

The store pushes the filters of map and WFS requests into the read. A Parquet file stores its rows in blocks called row groups, and the values of a column inside a row group in pages. The read skips the row groups and pages unable to match the filter, and fetches the rest with byte-range requests. At small map scales, it also skips the parts of the files landing on pixels already drawn.

The reads of the layers share memory budgets sized from the memory limit of the container. A full budget slows a read down instead of killing the server (Why Parquetry?).

items.title: Prepare the files
items.text: The store reads any Parquet file. GeoParquet files sorted by location, with a page index and bounding box columns, filter best. Parquetry's writer and the par command line tool produce them (Lay out files for selective queries).

items.title: Status
items.text: The "Parquet" store is stable. The module also has a STAC GeoParquet store and an Apache Iceberg store, both experimental (The other stores of the module).

items.title: GeoServer Cloud
items.text:
You run GeoServer Cloud 3.1.0 or newer and want to publish GeoParquet files as layers, or to hand layers to an analytics tool. GeoServer Cloud includes Parquetry and enables it by default: a store created through the REST API gives layers that you can see in the layer preview, and WFS downloads any vector layer as a GeoParquet file or an Arrow IPC stream.

The GeoServer Cloud user guide covers both tasks step by step. This page says what they give you, and where Parquetry's own pages help.

items.title: What is enabled
items.text:
In GeoServer Cloud 3.1.0 and newer, these are enabled by default:

  • the Parquetry extension and its "Parquet" data store, which reads GeoParquet files;
  • the geoparquet and arrow-ipc output formats of WFS GetFeature.

The STAC GeoParquet and Iceberg stores of Parquetry are not ready for production yet, and ship disabled (The experimental stores).

items.title: Publish GeoParquet files as layers
items.text:
The guide GeoParquet through the REST API creates a workspace, a "Parquet" store and its layers with curl. The store points at a file, a directory or a glob of files, on a local volume, an HTTP server, Amazon S3 or an S3-compatible service, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage. Its layers are read-only.

The store has the parameters of the GeoTools data store: geoparquet for the location, layer-grouping to publish a directory as one layer or one layer per file, fid for the feature ids, and the storage.* parameters of the backend. The byte ranges read from remote storage are cached in memory by default.

The filters of WMS and WFS requests on these layers run inside the read, which skips the parts of the files unable to match (Filters pushed into the read). Files sorted by location, with a page index and bounding box columns, filter best (Lay out files for selective queries).

items.title: Download layers as GeoParquet or Arrow IPC
items.text:
The guide GeoParquet and Arrow IPC over WFS downloads layers with the geoparquet and arrow-ipc WFS output formats, and reads them with DuckDB, pyarrow and GeoPandas.

These formats apply to any vector layer, whatever its store: PostGIS, shapefiles, GeoPackage or GeoParquet. The WFS request filters the features in that store, and the download holds the result. An analytics engine such as DuckDB then receives columnar input, already narrowed to the features and attributes of the request. Parquetry is not an analytics engine itself; Feed an analytics engine explains the split.

items.title: Next to the DuckDB-based store
items.text: GeoServer also has a GeoParquet community module, based on DuckDB, named "GeoParquet". The Parquetry store is independent of it, and the two can run side by side in GeoServer Cloud. Why Parquetry? tells why Parquetry was started for this deployment.

items.title: The experimental stores
items.text: The STAC GeoParquet and Iceberg stores are hidden while the system properties parquetry.geotools.stac-geoparquet.disabled and parquetry.geotools.iceberg.disabled are true. GeoServer Cloud sets both at startup, unless they are already set. Start the JVM with -Dparquetry.geotools.iceberg.disabled=false, or the STAC GeoParquet equivalent, to turn one of them on.

items.title: Size the pods
items.text: Parquetry sizes the memory of its reads from the memory limit of the pod, and shares it between the layers. Size a GeoServer pod gives two pod profiles and the settings beside them.

items.title: The GeoServer plugin
items.text:
You run GeoServer and want to publish GeoParquet files as map layers. The Parquetry plugin, from the tileverse-geoserver project, adds the Parquetry stores to GeoServer. Once it is installed, "Parquet" appears among the vector data sources of the new store page, and a layer published from it shows in the layer preview.

GeoServer Cloud 3.1.0 and newer include Parquetry, with the same stores and output formats: see GeoServer Cloud instead.

items.title: Install the plugin
items.text:
The plugin needs GeoServer running on Java 25, started with --enable-preview --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED (Runtime requirements).

The releases of tileverse-geoserver provide one plugin zip per GeoServer series. The notes of a release name the GeoServer version and the Parquetry version included in it. Unzip the plugin into webapps/geoserver/WEB-INF/lib and restart GeoServer. A release also has a demo zip: a GeoServer with the plugin and sample data, needing only Docker.

The tileverse-geoserver README describes the build from source and the Maven coordinates.

items.title: What the plugin adds
items.text:
The data access code is the GeoTools data store of Parquetry. The plugin adds what GeoServer needs around it:

  • Store pages. The page of a store shows the storage settings: a choice of backend, the fields of the chosen backend, and secrets masked.
  • WFS output formats. geoparquet and arrow-ipc download the result of a WFS GetFeature request as a GeoParquet file or as an Arrow IPC stream, for any vector layer of GeoServer.
  • Module status. The stores and output formats have their own rows under About, Server Status, Modules.

Three more features are merged for the next plugin release, the first one built with Parquetry 1.0-RC6:

  • The byte-range cache on the store page. The page shows the memory cache of the byte ranges read from remote storage, on by default.
  • A file browser. A "Browse..." button next to the location lists one folder of the storage at a time. For a .parquet file it shows the rows, the row groups (blocks of rows of the file), the geometry column, the coordinate reference system and the GeoParquet version.
  • Cache reset. A reset or a reload of GeoServer clears the caches of Parquetry: the file footers, the page indexes and the byte ranges.

The plugin is licensed under the GNU General Public License, version 2 or later, as GeoServer is. Parquetry itself is licensed under the Apache License, version 2.0.

items.title: The stores
items.text:
The plugin offers three stores:

  • Parquet publishes Parquet and GeoParquet files and directories. It is the stable store of the family.
  • The Iceberg and STAC stores read Apache Iceberg tables and STAC GeoParquet collections. They are experimental.

A system property hides a store from GeoServer (The other stores of the module).

GeoServer also has a GeoParquet community module, based on DuckDB, named "GeoParquet" in the store list. The two are separate stores and can be installed together. The Parquetry store is the one named "Parquet".

items.title: Where to go next
items.text:
• The GeoTools data store lists the connection parameters and the filters pushed into the read.
  • Size a GeoServer pod gives the memory and CPU of a pod serving Parquetry layers.
  • Lay out files for selective queries describes the files that filter best.

items.title: The GeoTools data store
items.text: You build a service on GeoTools and want to serve GeoParquet files as feature sources. The parquetry-geotools module registers a read-only GeoTools data store, named "Parquet", which DataStoreFinder opens from one parameter: the location of a file or a directory. GeoServer and GeoServer Cloud publish layers through the same store.

items.title: Open a store
items.text:
Add the module to a project importing the Parquetry BOM, as in Getting started:

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.tileverse.parquetry</groupId>
  <artifactId>parquetry-geotools</artifactId>
</dependency>

The module declares GeoTools as a provided dependency: the application brings its own gt-main. The module is compiled against GeoTools 35. GeoTools is published to the OSGeo repository, https://repo.osgeo.org/repository/release/: declare it in the repositories of your POM. A file declaring its coordinate reference system with an EPSG code also needs an EPSG authority on the classpath, such as gt-epsg-hsql. GeoServer includes one.

The program opens the countries.parquet file of Getting started and prints the countries whose geometry crosses a box over Kansas:

import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.Map;
import org.geotools.api.data.DataStore;
import org.geotools.api.data.DataStoreFinder;
import org.geotools.api.data.Query;
import org.geotools.api.data.SimpleFeatureSource;
import org.geotools.api.feature.simple.SimpleFeature;
import org.geotools.api.filter.Filter;
import org.geotools.api.filter.FilterFactory;
import org.geotools.data.simple.SimpleFeatureCollection;
import org.geotools.data.simple.SimpleFeatureIterator;
import org.geotools.factory.CommonFactoryFinder;

public class CountriesInBox {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Map<String, Object> params = Map.of("geoparquet", "file:///data/countries.parquet");
        DataStore store = DataStoreFinder.getDataStore(params);
        try {
            String typeName = store.getTypeNames()[0];
            SimpleFeatureSource countries = store.getFeatureSource(typeName);

            FilterFactory filters = CommonFactoryFinder.getFilterFactory();
            Filter inBox = filters.bbox("geometry", -100, 35, -95, 40, null);
            Query query = new Query(typeName, inBox, "name", "pop_est");

            SimpleFeatureCollection features = countries.getFeatures(query);
            try (SimpleFeatureIterator iterator = features.features()) {
                while (iterator.hasNext()) {
                    SimpleFeature country = iterator.next();
                    System.out.println(country.getAttribute("name"));
                }
            }
        } finally {
            store.dispose();
        }
    }
}

It prints United States of America. The store has one layer, named after the file: countries. The bounding box has no coordinate reference system, and the store takes it in the coordinate reference system of the file. The read decodes the columns needed by the filter and by the two requested attributes, and none of the others.

items.title: Connection parameters
items.text:
Parameter Required Meaning geoparquet yes The URI of a Parquet file or of a directory, such as file:///data/countries.parquet or s3://my-bucket/countries/, or a glob, such as s3://my-bucket/countries/*.parquet. Its presence selects this store. layer-grouping no For a directory: merged (the default) or file, described below. fid no The column holding the feature ids (Feature ids). namespace no The namespace URI of the feature types. storage.provider no The storage backend, such as file, http, s3, azure or gcs. By default, the scheme of the location selects it. storage.caching.enabled no Whether the store keeps the byte ranges read from remote storage in memory. On by default since Parquetry 1.0-RC6, off before. Local files have no byte-range cache.

The other storage.* parameters hold the credentials and the settings of the backends, such as storage.s3.region. The tileverse guides Authenticate and Use each backend list them. The S3, Azure and Google Cloud Storage backends are separate modules: add tileverse-storage-all, or the module of one backend, as in Cloud storage. The parameter list of the store shows the backends found on the classpath.

A Parquet file without geometry columns opens too, as a layer without geometry.

items.title: Directories and layers
items.text:
A single file is always one layer. A directory gives layers by the layer-grouping parameter:

  • merged reads the .parquet files under the directory, at any depth, as one layer. The files must have the same schema. A tree of Hive partitions, with directories such as year=2024/, fits this mode, and its partition values become columns (Multi-file datasets).
  • file publishes the .parquet files at the top of the directory as layers of their own, named after their files. The files may have different schemas, as in a directory holding one file per theme. This mode does not look into subdirectories: a tree of Hive partitions has no file at its top, and opening it fails with "no files found".

A store over files with different schemas in merged mode fails when a layer is first read, and the error names the layer-grouping parameter.

items.title: Filters pushed into the read
items.text:
The store translates the filter of a GeoTools query into a Parquetry predicate, and the read evaluates it. The read skips the row groups (blocks of rows of a file) and the pages (runs of values of one column inside a row group) unable to match, before fetching them (Selective queries read little):

  • Spatial filters are pushed exactly: BBOX, Intersects, Contains, Within, Crosses, Overlaps, Touches, Disjoint, Equals, and DWithin without distance units. The read tests the geometries with JTS, and GeoTools does not test them again. The pruning uses the bounding box of the query geometry (Filter by location). A filter with two boxes, as sent by a map renderer for a map crossing the antimeridian, prunes the two boxes separately.
  • Attribute filters are pushed: comparisons, BETWEEN, IS NULL, and their combinations with AND, OR and NOT. On a FLOAT attribute, only equality is pushed; other comparisons stay with GeoTools.
  • Temporal filters on a timestamp attribute, such as AFTER, BEFORE and DURING, are pushed as comparisons with the instant or the bounds of the period.
  • Other filters, such as LIKE and functions, stay with GeoTools, which tests the features returned by the read.

A spatial filter must be in the coordinate reference system of the data: the store rejects a geometry in another one. GeoServer reprojects the filters of its requests before they reach the store.

DWithin is pushed when it has no distance units, and its distance is then in the units of the data. A DWithin with units stays with GeoTools, which tests the features returned by the read. A query keeping such a filter is counted and bounded by reading its features, and gets no skipping of drawn pixels (Maps at small scales).

The store also pushes the rest of the query:

  • The read decodes the columns of the requested attributes, plus the columns needed by the filters left to GeoTools.
  • A feature limit (maxFeatures) stops the read once enough features are returned.
  • When the whole filter is pushed, a count comes from the read without building features, and the bounds of a query come from the statistics of the files when they have them.

items.title: Maps at small scales
items.text: When GeoServer draws a map at a small scale, many features fall on the same pixel. The renderer passes the store a map of the pixels already drawn, and the store gives it to the read when the whole filter is pushed. The read skips the files, row groups and pages smaller than a pixel whose bounding box falls on drawn pixels, without fetching them. It drops the features smaller than a pixel that land on a drawn pixel. When the map needs the geometry alone, a small part of a file lying inside the query may be drawn as one pixel-sized shape instead of being fetched.

items.title: Feature ids
items.text:
The store takes the feature ids from:

  1. The column named by the fid parameter, when set. It must be a string, numeric or UUID column, not a geometry, or the store fails to open the layer.
  2. Otherwise, a column named id, when the file has one of those types.
  3. Otherwise, sequence numbers given to the features by the read.

With a feature id column, Id filters work, and the read uses them to skip row groups and pages. Sequence numbers change between reads: the store rejects an Id filter on such a layer with an error, rather than returning wrong features.

items.title: Attribute types
items.text:
Parquet column Attribute type BOOLEAN, INT32, INT64, FLOAT, DOUBLE Boolean, Integer, Long, Float, Double DATE LocalDate TIMESTAMP, adjusted to UTC or not Instant or LocalDateTime TIME LocalTime DECIMAL BigDecimal at the scale of the column; byte[] for a DECIMAL stored as BYTE_ARRAY BYTE_ARRAY holding strings, or other bytes String or byte[] UUID UUID A struct, a map or a list Map or List A geometry column a JTS geometry, in the coordinate reference system declared by the file

An INT96 column, the legacy timestamp of Spark and Impala files, is left out of the feature type.

The bbox covering column of a GeoParquet file is not an attribute. A geometry column without a declared coordinate reference system is read as OGC:CRS84, the GeoParquet default. A coordinate reference system unknown to GeoTools leaves the attribute without one, and the store logs it.

A timestamp without a time zone is read as UTC. The store registers a GeoTools converter for the java.time types: filters can compare these attributes with a Date, an ISO 8601 text or an OGC temporal literal.

items.title: Runtime requirements
items.text: The store reads its files through parquetry-catalog, compiled with Java 25 preview features. Run GeoTools or GeoServer on Java 25, with --enable-preview --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED. A JVM of another version, or started without --enable-preview, cannot load these classes. Getting started explains both flags.

items.title: The other stores of the module
items.text:
The module registers two more stores. The STAC GeoParquet store, selected by the stac-geoparquet parameter, opens a STAC catalog.json or a stac-geoparquet table of items. The Apache Iceberg store, selected by the iceberg parameter, opens an Iceberg table or a warehouse of tables. Both are experimental, and GeoServer Cloud ships them disabled. STAC GeoParquet collections and Apache Iceberg tables describe what they read.

A system property set to true hides a store from DataStoreFinder: parquetry.geotools.geoparquet.disabled, parquetry.geotools.stac-geoparquet.disabled or parquetry.geotools.iceberg.disabled.

items.title: Write features as GeoParquet
items.text: GeoParquetExporter.export(features, out, options) writes a GeoTools feature collection to an output stream as a GeoParquet file. The geoparquet WFS output format of the GeoServer plugin uses it. Write files describes the write options.

items.title: Under the hood
items.text:
• Spatial filtering explains how a spatial filter prunes and tests rows.
  • The read path follows a filtered read from the footer to the rows.
  • Memory explains the memory budgets shared by the layers of a server.

items.title: Size a GeoServer pod
items.text: You deploy GeoServer or GeoServer Cloud in containers and want to choose the CPU and memory of a pod serving Parquetry layers. Parquetry sizes the memory of its reads from the memory limit of the pod, and no setting is needed per layer. This page gives two pod profiles and the arithmetic behind them.

items.title: How Parquetry follows the pod
items.text:
At startup, Parquetry reads the memory limit of the container and the maximum heap of the JVM. The difference is the memory left beside the heap. Parquetry takes its two native memory budgets from it:

  • the fetch budget, a fifth of it, bounds the column data fetched by the reads;
  • the off-heap decode budget, half of it, bounds the decoded values kept outside the heap.

The layers of the pod share these budgets. Adding a layer adds nothing to tune. When the fetch budget is full, a read waits for room, then writes its buffers to a temporary file: the read slows down, and the pod keeps its size. A read fails with an error only when the disk budget is full too, and the other requests keep running.

The caches of Parquetry, the file footers and the byte ranges read from remote storage, are on the Java heap, inside -Xmx.

Parquetry decodes on a shared pool of threads, one per CPU seen by the JVM. The JVM counts the CPU limit of the container.

Memory explains the budgets, and Tune memory shows their settings.

items.title: Two profiles
items.text:
Profile CPU Memory Small 4 CPU 4 GB Recommended 8 cores 16 GB

The two profiles differ in size only. Parquetry applies the same rules to both, and the next section gives their budgets.

items.title: The budgets of the profiles
items.text:
The table applies the rules above to both profiles, for a heap at half the container, as set for example by -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50. The figures are approximate.

Small, 4 GB Recommended, 16 GB Maximum heap 2 GB 8 GB Memory beside the heap 2 GB 8 GB Fetch budget, a fifth 400 MB 1.6 GB Off-heap decode budget, half 1 GB 4 GB Left for the pages being decoded, the JVM and the page cache 600 MB 2.4 GB

The two budgets take at most 35% of the container. Sizing against a container limit gives the full formula.

items.title: Settings to check
items.text:
• Mind the heap size. The budgets take their share of the memory left beside the heap. A heap above half the container shrinks them, and more fetches go to spill files. With a heap close to the container limit, the budgets still derive from an eighth of the container. The heap, the budgets, the decoded pages and the JVM itself may then need more memory than the container allows.
  • Put the spill files on disk. Spill files go to java.io.tmpdir by default, and parquetry.io.spillDir moves them. A directory on a memory-backed file system, such as a Kubernetes emptyDir volume with medium: Memory, counts against the memory limit of the pod (Change the memory figure).
  • Allow native access. Start the JVM with --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED. Parquetry allocates its large buffers as memory mappings, and returns their memory to the system as soon as it frees them. The flag keeps the JDK from warning about them (Allow native access).
  • Size the caches inside the heap. The tileverse cache settings size the footer and byte-range caches (Size the caches). A store turns its byte-range cache off with storage.caching.enabled=false.
  • Override the memory figure only when needed. parquetry.io.maxOffHeap, or the environment variable PARQUETRY_IO_MAX_OFFHEAP, replaces the memory beside the heap measured at startup.

items.title: Under the hood
items.text:
• Memory explains the budgets, their defaults and the caches.
  • Native memory and spill explains the wait and the spill files.

items.title: Arrow interop
items.text:
You want to analyze the data of a Parquet file with an engine such as DuckDB, Polars, DataFusion or pandas, and let Parquetry do the reading. Parquetry exports a read as Apache Arrow, the in-memory columnar format read by these engines. The engine receives the rows left after Parquetry's pruning and filtering, and runs the query on them.

It needs parquetry-arrow. Getting started imports the BOM, which sets the version of the module.

items.title: The IPC writer
items.text:
An Arrow IPC stream is a byte stream of Arrow data, to write to a file, a socket or a pipe. ArrowIpcWriter writes the batches of a read to an output stream. The program writes the countries.parquet file of Getting started to countries.arrows:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.arrow.ipc.ArrowIpcWriter;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.columnar.ParquetRecordBatch;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ParquetFileReader;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ReadOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Projection;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.io.ByteRangeSource;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.geo.geoparquet.GeoParquetMetadata;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.io.OutputStream;
import java.nio.file.Files;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class ExportCountries {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        Path path = Path.of("countries.parquet");
        Path output = Path.of("countries.arrows");

        try (ByteRangeSource source = ByteRangeSource.ofFile(path);
                OutputStream out = Files.newOutputStream(output)) {
            ParquetFileReader reader = ParquetFileReader.open(source);
            String geoJson = reader.keyValueMetadata().get("geo");
            Optional<GeoParquetMetadata> geo = Optional.ofNullable(geoJson).map(GeoParquetMetadata::parse);
            try (Stream<ParquetRecordBatch> batches =
                    reader.readBatches(Predicate.ALWAYS_TRUE, Projection.ALL, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS)) {
                ArrowIpcWriter.write(reader.schema(), geo, batches, out);
            }
        }
    }
}

write takes the schema of the batches, the GeoParquet metadata of the file when it has one, the batches, and the output. The sample reads the columns of the file and passes the schema of the file. A read with a projection passes the schema of the projected columns instead. The schema is checked before any byte is written: an unsupported column fails the write at once. The OutputStream overload flushes but does not close the stream; the WritableByteChannel overload neither flushes nor closes.

From the CLI:

par cat data.parquet -o arrow > data.arrows

items.title: Feed an analytics engine
items.text:
Parquetry is not an analytics engine: it reads, filters and writes files, and runs no SQL, joins or aggregations. It can feed an engine. Its Arrow IPC output gives an engine such as DuckDB columnar input, already narrowed to the rows and columns of the read.

DuckDB reads Arrow IPC streams through the nanoarrow community extension. With DuckDB 2.0.0, this command reads the countries.arrows file written above:

duckdb -c "install nanoarrow from community; load nanoarrow;
  install spatial; load spatial;
  select name, pop_est, ST_GeometryType(geometry) as type
  from read_arrow('countries.arrows') where pop_est > 100000000;"

It returns one row: United States of America, 328239523.0, MULTIPOLYGON. DuckDB reads the geometry column as geometries, from its geoarrow.wkb tag (GeoArrow).

Through GeoServer, the same output reaches beyond GeoParquet files. The arrow-ipc and geoparquet WFS output formats, added by Parquetry to GeoServer Cloud, apply to any vector layer, whatever store is behind it: PostGIS, shapefiles, GeoPackage or GeoParquet. The WFS request filters the features in that store, and the engine receives the result. The GeoServer Cloud guide GeoParquet and Arrow IPC over WFS downloads a layer in both formats and reads it with DuckDB and pyarrow.

items.title: Two forms: IPC and the C Data Interface
items.text:
Arrow defines two unrelated ways to move columnar data, and Parquetry implements both because they answer different questions.

  • Arrow IPC stream (ArrowIpcWriter) is the serialization format: a framed byte stream of flatbuffer messages - one Schema message, then one RecordBatch message per batch, then an end-of-stream marker. It is bytes you write to a file, a socket, or a pipe and read back somewhere else: another process, another language, or later in time. The writer converts the batches to Arrow's buffer layout, and writes those buffers to the channel without copying them again. See the IPC streaming format.
  • Arrow C Data Interface (ArrowCDataExporter) is an in-process ABI: a small set of C structs (ArrowSchema, ArrowArray, and the streaming ArrowArrayStream) that let two components in the same process share Arrow data by passing pointers, without serialization. The consumer reads the producer's buffers directly by address; a release callback on each struct hands ownership back when the consumer is done. Parquetry fills an ArrowArrayStream, and a native consumer pulls batches from it (DuckDB registerArrowStream, Polars, or any C Data consumer). See the C Data Interface and the C Stream Interface.

The short version: reach for the IPC stream to persist or send Arrow across a boundary, and the C Data Interface to hand Arrow to another library running in the same JVM process without serialization. The C Data exporter converts each batch to Arrow's buffer layout, as the IPC writer does, then copies each buffer once into pooled native memory, held until the consumer releases the batch (Lifecycle and ownership). Both are driven from the same columnar read path and the same Parquet-to-Arrow type mapping below.

Parquetry's read path produces columnar batches (ParquetRecordBatch). The Arrow exporters reshape those batches into Arrow's layout. Both forms are read-path only; the Parquet writer is not involved.

items.title: The C Data Interface exporter
items.text:
The caller provides an allocated ArrowArrayStream struct (for example arrow-java's ArrowArrayStream.allocateNew, or a raw FFM segment) and Parquetry fills its callbacks. The program hands the rows of countries.parquet to DuckDB through its JDBC driver, and prints the countries with more than 100 million inhabitants:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.arrow.cdi.ArrowCDataExporter;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.columnar.ParquetRecordBatch;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ParquetFileReader;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ReadOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Projection;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.io.ByteRangeSource;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.geo.geoparquet.GeoParquetMetadata;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.sql.DriverManager;
import java.sql.ResultSet;
import java.sql.SQLException;
import java.sql.Statement;
import java.util.Optional;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import org.apache.arrow.c.ArrowArrayStream;
import org.apache.arrow.memory.BufferAllocator;
import org.apache.arrow.memory.RootAllocator;
import org.duckdb.DuckDBConnection;

public class QueryWithDuckDb {

    public static void main(String[] args) throws SQLException {
        Path path = Path.of("countries.parquet");

        try (ByteRangeSource source = ByteRangeSource.ofFile(path);
                BufferAllocator allocator = new RootAllocator();
                ArrowArrayStream stream = ArrowArrayStream.allocateNew(allocator);
                DuckDBConnection connection = (DuckDBConnection) DriverManager.getConnection("jdbc:duckdb:")) {
            ParquetFileReader reader = ParquetFileReader.open(source);
            String geoJson = reader.keyValueMetadata().get("geo");
            Optional<GeoParquetMetadata> geo = Optional.ofNullable(geoJson).map(GeoParquetMetadata::parse);
            Stream<ParquetRecordBatch> batches =
                    reader.readBatches(Predicate.ALWAYS_TRUE, Projection.ALL, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS);
            ArrowCDataExporter.export(reader.schema(), geo, batches, stream.memoryAddress());
            connection.registerArrowStream("countries", stream);
            try (Statement statement = connection.createStatement();
                    ResultSet result =
                            statement.executeQuery("SELECT name FROM countries WHERE pop_est > 100000000")) {
                while (result.next()) {
                    System.out.println(result.getString("name"));
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

It prints United States of America. Beside parquetry-arrow, the sample needs three modules, with their versions set by parquetry-dependencies (Getting started): org.apache.arrow:arrow-c-data, an allocation manager of arrow-java such as org.apache.arrow:arrow-memory-unsafe, and org.duckdb:duckdb_jdbc. Without an allocation manager, new RootAllocator() fails.

On Java 25, the JVM of the application needs three flags:

java --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED \
    --add-opens=java.base/java.nio=ALL-UNNAMED \
    --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow \
    -cp <class path> QueryWithDuckDb
  • --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED lets the exporter and DuckDB call native code. Without it, the JDK prints warnings.
  • --add-opens=java.base/java.nio=ALL-UNNAMED is required by arrow-java. Without it, ArrowArrayStream.allocateNew fails.
  • --sun-misc-unsafe-memory-access=allow lets arrow-memory-unsafe use sun.misc.Unsafe. Without it, the JDK prints deprecation warnings.

The export takes the batch stream over: the consumer's release of the ArrowArrayStream closes it. The sample therefore leaves batches out of the try resources.

ArrowCDataExporter.export fills an ArrowArrayStream struct given its address. A caller that allocated the struct from its own FFM arena passes that MemorySegment to the segment overload instead.

items.title: Lifecycle and ownership
items.text:
The stream pulls lazily. get_next pulls the next ParquetRecordBatch on demand, converts it to Arrow's layout, copies it into pooled buffers, and returns it; the stream's release closes the batch stream. A single sequential stream still decodes ahead behind the get_next boundary.

A batch goes out in two steps. The exporter first builds the Arrow layout of the batch on the heap: the validity bitmaps, the offsets and the padded values, as the IPC writer does. It then copies each of these buffers once into a segment borrowed from a pool. The second copy is mandatory for the C Data Interface: a C consumer needs a stable native address, and heap buffers move and are recycled when the batch closes. The release of an exported array returns its buffers to the pool.

items.title: Consumer contract
items.text:
• A consumer drives get_schema once, then get_next until it returns an array whose release is null (end of stream), then release on the stream.
  • get_next is serialized internally; a consumer that parallelizes downstream work and release (DuckDB does) is safe, since each array owns its buffers and releases touch disjoint segments.
  • Releasing an array twice is a no-op.

items.title: Parquet to Arrow type mapping
items.text: Parquet Arrow type Notes BOOLEAN Bool INT32 Int32 signed INT32 INT(8/16/32, signed or unsigned) Int32 sign from the annotation, physical width kept INT64 Int64 unsigned INT(64,false) maps to UInt64 FLOAT / DOUBLE Float32 / Float64 FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY FLOAT16 Float16 BYTE_ARRAY STRING/ENUM/JSON Utf8 BYTE_ARRAY Binary FIXED_LEN_BYTE_ARRAY FixedSizeBinary(N) INT32 DATE Date32 (days) INT32/INT64 TIME Time32 / Time64 unit from the annotation INT64 TIMESTAMP Timestamp unit + UTC adjustment from the annotation INT96 Timestamp (micros, no tz) 12-byte value converted to int64 micros INT32/INT64/BYTE_ARRAY/FIXED DECIMAL Decimal128 unscaled value re-encoded 16-byte little-endian LIST group List element recurses MAP group Map list<struct<key, value>>; key field non-nullable struct group Struct one child per field Variant group Struct<metadata, value> tagged arrow.variant (see below) geometry / geography leaf Binary tagged geoarrow.wkb with crs/edges metadata

items.title: Variant
items.text: A Parquet Variant exports as Arrow struct<metadata: binary, value: binary> tagged with the arrow.variant extension name, following the geoarrow.wkb precedent. A shredded Variant is reconstructed to its unshredded canonical form on the way out. A consumer that does not interpret the extension (DuckDB) reads the two binary fields directly; an Arrow-native consumer can recognize the Variant from the tag.

items.title: GeoArrow
items.text: A geometry or geography column exports as geoarrow.wkb: Arrow Binary holding the WKB, with the ARROW:extension:name and an ARROW:extension:metadata JSON document recording the CRS and edge interpretation. Geometry is detected from the GeoParquet 2.0 logical type or from the GeoParquet 1.x geo metadata.

items.title: Documented limits
items.text:
• Decimal256 (DECIMAL precision 39-76) is rejected; the Arrow target is Decimal128 (precision up to 38).
  • Deeply-nested-shredded Variant (a Variant under a list or map) is rejected with a precise message. Top-level and struct-nested Variant are supported.
