items.title: Avro
items.text:
You have Avro object container files, such as the manifest files of an Iceberg table, and want to read or write them from Java without the Apache Avro library. parquetry-avro reads and writes these files. It is the Avro reader used by the Iceberg support of Parquetry, and it knows nothing about Iceberg itself. This guide writes a small file and reads it back.

It needs parquetry-avro, with the BOM imported as in Getting started:

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.tileverse.parquetry</groupId>
  <artifactId>parquetry-avro</artifactId>
</dependency>

The module depends on the byte sources and sinks of Parquetry, its compression codecs and jackson-core. It does not need parquetry-core.

items.title: Write and read a file
items.text:
The program writes two cities to cities.avro, then prints them:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.avro.AvroDataFileReader;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.avro.AvroDataFileWriter;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.avro.AvroRecord;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.io.ByteRangeSource;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.io.ByteSink;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.Map;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class WriteAndReadCities {

    private static final String SCHEMA = """
            {"type": "record", "name": "City", "fields": [
              {"name": "id", "type": "long"},
              {"name": "name", "type": ["null", "string"]}
            ]}
            """;

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Path path = Path.of("cities.avro");

        try (AvroDataFileWriter writer =
                AvroDataFileWriter.builder(SCHEMA).codec("deflate").build(ByteSink.ofFile(path))) {
            writer.write(Map.of("id", 1L, "name", "Rosario"));
            writer.write(Map.of("id", 2L, "name", "Montevideo"));
        }

        try (AvroDataFileReader reader = AvroDataFileReader.open(ByteRangeSource.ofFile(path));
                Stream<AvroRecord> records = reader.records()) {
            records.forEach(city -> System.out.println(city.get("id") + ": " + city.get("name")));
        }
    }
}

It prints:

1: Rosario
2: Montevideo

The writer and the reader own what they are given. Closing the writer writes the last block and closes the sink. Closing the reader closes the source.

items.title: Read records
items.text:
reader.records() returns a lazy stream of AvroRecord, read and decompressed one block of the file at a time. Each call returns a new stream starting at the first record. A record gives its values by field name, with get("name"), or by position, with get(0).

The values have these Java types:

Avro type Java type boolean, int, long, float, double Boolean, Integer, Long, Float, Double string String bytes, fixed a read-only MemorySegment record, array, map AvroRecord, List, Map the null branch of a union null decimal, uuid BigDecimal, UUID date, time-millis, time-micros LocalDate, LocalTime timestamp-millis, timestamp-micros Instant local-timestamp-millis, local-timestamp-micros LocalDateTime duration AvroDuration

An unknown logical type is read as its underlying type.

reader.schema() returns the schema written in the file, and reader.metadata() the metadata of its header, such as avro.codec. The schema keeps the custom attributes of the fields, such as the field-id of an Iceberg manifest: AvroSchema.Field.attributes() returns them as written. The doc attributes are not kept.

records() requires a record at the top level of the schema. schema() and metadata() work for any schema.

items.title: Read with another schema
items.text:
reader.records(readerSchema) reads the records with the schema expected by your code, following the schema resolution rules of the Avro specification. The fields missing from the reader schema are skipped, a field missing from the file takes its default, numbers are promoted, and aliases match renamed fields:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.avro.AvroSchema;

AvroSchema names = AvroSchema.parse("""
        {"type": "record", "name": "City", "fields": [
          {"name": "name", "type": ["null", "string"]},
          {"name": "country", "type": "string", "default": "unknown"}
        ]}
        """);
try (Stream<AvroRecord> records = reader.records(names)) {
    records.forEach(city -> System.out.println(city.get("name") + ", " + city.get("country")));
}

On cities.avro, it prints Rosario, unknown and Montevideo, unknown. A field of the reader schema without a match and without a default raises an AvroFormatException when the read reaches it.

items.title: Write records
items.text:
AvroDataFileWriter.builder(schemaJson) takes the schema as JSON, and writes it unchanged into the header of the file. write takes a record as a Map keyed by field name, or as an AvroRecord. The schema decides the type of each value. The writer widens numbers, such as an Integer for a long field, and rejects a value of another kind, such as a String for a number, with an AvroFormatException.

  • Codec. codec(name) compresses the blocks with null (no compression, the default), deflate, snappy, zstandard, bzip2 or xz. The reader reads the six.
  • Blocks. The writer writes a block when its records reach about 64 KiB. blockSize(bytes) changes the threshold.
  • Sync marker. The 16-byte marker between blocks is random. syncMarker(bytes) fixes it, for files identical from run to run.
  • Sink. build(sink) writes to any ByteSink. Closing the writer writes the last block and closes the sink.

The writer closes its sink, unlike the Parquet writer. For an upload to object storage, the sink is ByteSink.ofOutputStream over the upload stream of Cloud storage, and closing it publishes the object. An Avro file has no footer: a writer closed after a failure publishes a valid file missing records. Keep such a writer out of the try resources. Close it after the last record, and call abort() on the upload stream after a failure.

items.title: Limits
items.text:
The module does not implement Parsing Canonical Form, CRC-64-AVRO fingerprints, single-object encoding, Avro RPC, or the container format written before Avro 1.3.

The reader checks the nesting depth, the block counts and the sync markers of a file, and rejects a corrupt or hostile file with an AvroFormatException.

items.title: Cloud storage
items.text:
You have Parquet files on an HTTP server or in object storage, such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage, and want to query them from Java without downloading them first. Parquetry reads them through tileverse-storage and fetches only the byte ranges needed by the query. This guide reads the file of Getting started from its HTTPS address, then shows the other backends and how to write a file to object storage.

It needs parquetry-core, which reads local files and HTTP servers on its own. Getting started adds the dependency and lists the JVM flags.

items.title: Read a remote file
items.text:
The program runs the query of Getting started on the sample file of the GeoParquet specification, read from GitHub:

import static io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Pred.col;

import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ParquetFileReader;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ReadOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Projection;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.io.ByteRangeSource;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.record.ParquetRecord;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ColumnPath;
import io.tileverse.storage.Storage;
import io.tileverse.storage.StorageFactory;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.URI;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class ReadRemote {

    private static final ColumnPath NAME = ColumnPath.of("name");
    private static final ColumnPath POPULATION = ColumnPath.of("pop_est");

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        URI examples = URI.create("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/opengeospatial/geoparquet/v2.0.0/examples/");
        Predicate filter = col("pop_est").gtEq(100_000_000.0);
        Projection columns = Projection.ofPhysical(List.of(NAME, POPULATION));

        try (Storage storage = StorageFactory.open(examples);
                ByteRangeSource source = ByteRangeSource.owning(storage.openVersionedRangeReader("example.parquet"))) {
            ParquetFileReader reader = ParquetFileReader.open(source);
            try (Stream<ParquetRecord> rows = reader.read(filter, columns, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS)) {
                rows.forEach(ReadRemote::printCountry);
            }
        }
    }

    private static void printCountry(ParquetRecord row) {
        String name = row.getString(NAME);
        double population = row.getDouble(POPULATION);
        System.out.println(name + ": " + population);
    }
}

It prints United States of America: 3.28239523E8, as the local read of Getting started does. Only the opening of the file differs:

  • StorageFactory.open opens a tileverse Storage over a container: here the directory of the file on the server. Close it after the last stream of the read.
  • openVersionedRangeReader opens one file of the container by its key, and asks the server for the version of the file, such as its ETag.
  • ByteRangeSource.owning hands the file to Parquetry. Closing the source closes the tileverse reader.

From there, the read is the one of a local file. Parquetry reads the footer of the file, rules out the row groups and pages unable to match the filter, and fetches the rest with byte-range requests. A row group is a block of rows of the file, and a page is a smaller run of values of one column inside it.

items.title: Choose a backend
items.text:
The scheme of the URI selects the backend. Local files and HTTP come with parquetry-core, and the cloud backends have modules of their own:

URI Backend Module file: or a plain path Local file system included http:, https: HTTP server included s3://my-bucket/countries/ Amazon S3 and S3-compatible services tileverse-storage-s3 az://my-account/my-container/countries/, abfss: Azure Blob Storage, Azure Data Lake Storage tileverse-storage-azure gs://my-bucket/countries/ Google Cloud Storage tileverse-storage-gcs

Add the module of the backend to your dependencies. tileverse-storage-all adds the three. The parquetry-dependencies BOM, imported as in Getting started, sets their version:

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.tileverse.storage</groupId>
  <artifactId>tileverse-storage-s3</artifactId>
</dependency>

The program stays the same: pass URI.create("s3://my-bucket/countries/") to StorageFactory.open. Without the module of its scheme, the open fails. StorageFactory.open(uri, properties) takes the credentials and the other parameters of the backend, listed by the tileverse guides Authenticate and Use each backend.

items.title: What Parquetry keeps between reads
items.text:
Parquetry parses the footer of a file once and keeps it in a cache shared by the readers of the process. A later open of the same file reads no footer. The page indexes learned from the page headers of a file go in the same cache (Without a page index).

The cache keys a file by its URI, its version and its length. A reader opened with openVersionedRangeReader, or from an entry of a listing, knows the version of the file. A reader opened with openRangeReader(key) has no version. If a file of that kind is rewritten under the same name at the same length, reads get the old footer until it leaves the cache.

The byte ranges of the data are kept only when the Storage caches them. A Storage opened with storage.caching.enabled=true caches the ranges read through its readers:

import java.util.Properties;

Properties properties = new Properties();
properties.setProperty("storage.caching.enabled", "true");
Storage storage = StorageFactory.open(examples, properties);

The cache serves repeated reads of the same parts of a file, as made by a map server. The GeoTools data stores of Parquetry turn it on by default for remote files, and the store parameter storage.caching.enabled=false turns it off. par and the FileSource.open method of Multi-file datasets leave it off. The byte ranges of local files are not cached.

The tileverse guide Caching layers describes the caches and their settings. Tune memory sizes them against the heap. A read hands the byte ranges of a row group to tileverse-storage in one call, and tileverse-storage decides how to group them into requests (Batched reads).

items.title: Write to object storage
items.text:
A Storage also opens an upload stream, and the writer writes the file to it:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ParquetFileWriter;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ParquetRecordBatchBuilder;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ColumnPath;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ParquetSchema;
import io.tileverse.storage.Storage;
import io.tileverse.storage.StorageFactory;
import io.tileverse.storage.StorageOutputStream;
import io.tileverse.storage.WriteOptions;
import java.io.IOException;
import java.net.URI;

public class UploadCities {

    private static final ColumnPath ID = ColumnPath.of("id");
    private static final ColumnPath NAME = ColumnPath.of("name");

    public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException {
        URI exports = URI.create("s3://my-bucket/exports/");
        ParquetSchema schema = citySchema();

        try (Storage storage = StorageFactory.open(exports)) {
            StorageOutputStream upload = storage.openOutputStream("cities.parquet", WriteOptions.defaults());
            try (ParquetFileWriter writer = ParquetFileWriter.create(upload, schema);
                    ParquetRecordBatchBuilder rows = writer.appender()) {
                rows.setLong(ID, 1).setString(NAME, "Rosario").endRow();
                rows.setLong(ID, 2).setString(NAME, "Montevideo").endRow();
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                upload.abort();
                throw e;
            }
            upload.close();
        }
    }
}

citySchema() is the method of Write files. The sample leaves exports/cities.parquet with two rows.

  • Closing the upload publishes the object. The writer never closes the stream. The sample closes it after the writer closed without error, and the object appears complete.
  • On failure, abort. abort() discards the upload, and no object appears. Closing the stream instead would publish a file without a footer, or with the rows written before the failure.
  • Two WriteOptions. The WriteOptions of the sample are the options of the upload, from tileverse-storage. To pass Parquetry write options as well, write one of the two classes with its package name, such as io.tileverse.parquetry.data.WriteOptions.

The writer encodes the current row group into temporary files on the local disk, and appends it to the upload when it is complete. Tune memory chooses their directory.

  • Tune memory sizes the memory of the reads and the caches.

items.title: Under the hood
items.text: • The read path follows a filtered read from the footer to the fetched pages.

items.title: Multi-file datasets
items.text:
You have a directory, a bucket prefix or a Hive-partitioned tree of Parquet files sharing one schema, and want to query them as one table. parquetry-catalog reads them as one dataset: one count, one stream of rows, and the files unable to match the filter left unopened. This guide reads a directory of two files, then shows remote files, partitions, and one dataset per file.

It needs parquetry-catalog, with the BOM imported as in Getting started:

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.tileverse.parquetry</groupId>
  <artifactId>parquetry-catalog</artifactId>
</dependency>

parquetry-catalog uses Java 25 preview features: start the JVM with --enable-preview, as listed in Getting started.

items.title: Read a directory
items.text:
The directory cities holds two files written as in Write files, with an id and a name column. part-0.parquet holds Rosario and Montevideo, with the ids 1 and 2. part-1.parquet holds Asuncion and Santiago, with the ids 3 and 4. The program counts and prints the cities with an id of 3 or more:

import static io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Pred.col;

import io.tileverse.parquetry.catalog.CatalogOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.catalog.FilesetCatalog;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ReadOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.dataset.ParquetDataset;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Projection;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.io.FileSource;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.record.ParquetRecord;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ColumnPath;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class ReadDirectory {

    private static final ColumnPath NAME = ColumnPath.of("name");

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Path directory = Path.of("cities");
        Predicate filter = col("id").gtEq(3L);

        try (FileSource files = FileSource.directory(directory, "*.parquet");
                FilesetCatalog catalog = FilesetCatalog.open(files, CatalogOptions.defaults())) {
            String name = catalog.datasets().getFirst();
            ParquetDataset dataset = catalog.dataset(name);
            long matching = dataset.count(filter, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS);
            System.out.println(name + ": " + matching + " matching rows");
            try (Stream<ParquetRecord> rows = dataset.read(filter, Projection.ALL, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS)) {
                rows.forEach(row -> System.out.println(row.getString(NAME)));
            }
        }
    }
}

It prints:

cities: 2 matching rows
Asuncion
Santiago
  • FileSource.directory lists the files of the directory matching the glob. *.parquet matches the files of the directory itself, and **/*.parquet the files of its subdirectories too.
  • FilesetCatalog.open merges the listed files into one dataset, named after the directory. Opening the catalog reads no file. The first call to dataset(name) reads the footers of the files.
  • The dataset has the read methods of a single file: read, readBatches, count, bounds and explain, with the same predicates, projections and read options.
  • Closing the catalog closes the files and the source.

The files must have equal schemas. A file with another schema fails dataset(name) with a ParquetSchemaException naming the two files.

A read drains up to eight files at once, and the rows of different files come in no fixed order.

items.title: Skip files
items.text:
A dataset skips a file when the statistics in its footer rule it out, the way a single file skips row groups. explain shows the decisions on the files without reading the rows:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.dataset.explain.DatasetExplainPlan;

DatasetExplainPlan plan = dataset.explain(filter, Projection.ALL, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS);
System.out.println(plan.toAsciiTable());

For the filter of the sample, the plan starts with the files:

1 kept, 1 skipped  (2 rows pruned without opening a file)

location                                 outcome         rows   reason
part-0.parquet                           SKIP               2   GtEq id: value outside [min, max]
part-1.parquet                           KEEP               2   kept

The ids of part-0.parquet lie between 1 and 2, and the read never opens it. A kept file is read like a single file, skipping row groups and pages, and the plan lists these decisions after the files.

items.title: Read files from object storage
items.text:
FileSource.open takes the URI of a directory or a bucket prefix, and a glob:

import java.net.URI;
import java.util.Properties;

URI cities = URI.create("s3://my-bucket/cities/");
FileSource files = FileSource.open(cities, "**/*.parquet", new Properties());

A file: URI, or a URI without a scheme, names a local directory. Another scheme opens a tileverse Storage with the backend modules of Cloud storage, configured by the storage.* entries of the properties. The byte-range cache stays off unless the properties set storage.caching.enabled=true.

FileSource.openObject(uri, properties) serves one known object without listing its prefix. A credential allowed to read the object, and not to list the bucket, is enough.

items.title: Skip partitions
items.text:
A Hive-partitioned tree puts partition keys and their values in the names of its directories, as key=value:

cities/
  country=AR/part-0.parquet
  country=UY/part-0.parquet

FileSource.directory(directory, "**/*.parquet") lists both files, and the catalog reads them as one dataset. A filter on the key skips the files of the other partitions without opening them. With col("country").eq("UY"), the plan shows:

location                                 outcome         rows   reason
country=AR/part-0.parquet                SKIP               2   Eq country: value outside [min, max]
country=UY/part-0.parquet                KEEP               2   kept

The files of the sample have no country column. The dataset then adds one, after the columns of the files. For the rows of a file, the added column holds the value written in the path of that file. Its type comes from the values in the paths: whole numbers, decimal numbers, dates written as yyyy-MM-dd, or strings otherwise. A file with a country column of its own keeps it, and the path value prunes that column.

Such an added column cannot hold null partitions: a path segment country=__HIVE_DEFAULT_PARTITION__ fails dataset(name) with an IllegalStateException.

items.text: FilesetCatalog.openPerFile(files) makes each listed file a dataset of its own, named after the file without its extension. The files need not share a schema. Over a directory holding rivers.parquet and lakes.parquet, catalog.datasets() returns [lakes, rivers].

items.title: Lay out files for selective queries
items.text: You write GeoParquet files that will be queried by small bounding boxes, or Parquet files queried by narrow ranges of a key. With the layout below, such a query fetches the few pages near its answer instead of whole blocks of the file. Parquetry's writer produces this layout by default, except for the order of the rows.

items.title: The recommended layout
items.text:
A Parquet file stores its rows in row groups, blocks of rows described in the footer at the end of the file. Inside a row group, the values of a column sit together in a column chunk, cut into pages. Selective queries read little shows these parts in a diagram.

  • Write a page index. The page index records the position, minimum and maximum of the pages of a column chunk. A read uses it to skip the pages unable to match the filter, and fetches only the pages left. Without a page index, a first read by Parquetry fetches the whole column chunks of the row groups left. Later reads can prune pages learned from their headers, as described in Without a page index.
  • Keep the pages small on the filter columns. A read skips whole pages, and a small page lets it skip closer to the answer. For a spatial query, the filter columns are the bbox covering columns, four columns holding the bounding box of each geometry. Their values are short, four or eight bytes, and small pages on them add little to the size of the file.
  • Write the rows in spatial order. The minimum and maximum of a page rule it out only when its rows lie close together. Sorting the rows along a space-filling curve, such as a Hilbert curve, puts nearby geometries in the same pages and row groups. When the rows are in random order, the pages span most of the map and the page index rules out nothing.
  • Size row groups by bytes. The footer describes the row groups and their column chunks, and a reader parses the whole footer before it can run a query. Large row groups keep the footer small, and the page index provides the fine pruning. A size in bytes gives row groups of large polygons and row groups of points a similar weight.

A query on a range of keys follows the same rules, with the key column as the filter column: sort the rows by the key, and keep its pages small when the ranges are narrow.

items.title: Write the layout with the par command line tool
items.text:
par cp copies a file into this layout. The copy has a page index, covering columns in pages of at most 1,024 values, and row groups of about 128 MB of uncompressed data:

par cp places.parquet places-indexed.parquet

A source without bbox covering columns gets them in the copy. Write a GeoParquet file describes the covering written by Parquetry.

The options of par cp change the layout:

  • --covering-page-values <n> sets the number of values in a page of the covering columns. Smaller pages narrow a small box to fewer rows, and make the file and its page index slightly larger.
  • --row-group-bytes <size> sets the size of a row group in uncompressed bytes, such as 256MB. --row-group-rows <n> sets a row count instead.

par cp keeps the order of the source rows. Sort the rows before the copy, for example with DuckDB 2.0.0 and its spatial extension:

INSTALL spatial;
LOAD spatial;
COPY (
    SELECT * EXCLUDE (bbox) FROM 'places.parquet'
    ORDER BY ST_Hilbert(geometry, ST_Extent(ST_MakeEnvelope(-180, -90, 180, 90)))
) TO 'sorted.parquet';

The envelope is the extent of the coordinates, here longitude and latitude. The query leaves out the bbox column of the source, and par cp derives new covering columns for the copy. A kept bbox struct becomes the covering of the copy only when it follows the GeoParquet rules (Choose the GeoParquet metadata). For a source without a bbox column, remove EXCLUDE (bbox). par cp sorted.parquet places-indexed.parquet then writes the copy.

par explain shows the effect of the layout. With a filter such as --filter "ST_Intersects(geometry, ST_MakeEnvelope(10, 45, 11, 46))", its ColIdx column gives, per row group, the rows left after the page index.

items.title: Write the layout from Java
items.text:
The default write options produce the layout for a geometry column declared with a coordinate reference system:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.WriteOptions;

WriteOptions options = WriteOptions.builder()
        .crsEpsg("geometry", 4326)
        .coveringPageValueLimit(1024)
        .build();
  • crsEpsg declares geometry as a geometry column. The writer adds the bbox covering columns for it.
  • coveringPageValueLimit(n) sets the number of values in a page of the covering columns. The call repeats the default, 1,024. pageValueLimit(column, n) sets the page size of another column, such as a key column.
  • The writer writes a page index for Parquet 2.0 files, the default. A file written with parquetVersion(ParquetVersion.V1_1) has no page index.
  • Row groups hold about 128 MB of uncompressed data when the options give no expected row count. expectedRowCount(n) lets the writer pick larger row groups for large files, and rowGroupSize(RowGroupSize.bytes(n)) sets the size.
  • The writer keeps the order of the appended rows. Sort them before writing.

Write files shows a complete program, and its options table lists the other settings.

items.title: Write the layout with other tools
items.text:
A copy through par cp gives a file written by another tool a page index and covering columns. Other tools can also write them directly:

  • pyarrow 26.0.1 writes no page index by default, and writes one with write_page_index=True.
  • Writers should leave geometry out of dictionary encoding. Dictionary encoding stores the distinct values of a column once, and WKB geometries rarely repeat. pyarrow 26.0.1 tries a dictionary on each column by default (use_dictionary=True). In a file of building footprints, the dictionary of the geometry chunk holds one entry per row, and the chunk then falls back to plain encoding. use_dictionary takes a list of columns, and the columns with repeated values keep their dictionary. Parquetry's writer writes geometry columns without a dictionary unless told otherwise.

items.title: Why advice elsewhere centers on row-group size
items.text:
Guides written for other tools often recommend small row groups for selective queries. The advice follows from the readers targeted by those guides. A reader without page index support skips whole row groups. In a row group kept by the footer statistics, it fetches the column chunks of the queried columns whole. For such a reader, a smaller row group is the only way to fetch less under a selective query.

DuckDB 2.0.0, its latest release when this page was written, reads files this way. It read a file written by par cp from an HTTP server: it skipped row groups with the footer statistics, and fetched the whole column chunks of the row group left, although the file had a page index. DuckDB 2.0.0 writes files without a page index. DuckDB merged page index reading and writing after that release, in pull request 27326.

Small row groups have a cost for any reader. The footer grows with the number of row groups, and a reader parses the whole footer when it opens the file. A page index narrows a query below the row group without growing the footer. It sits in its own section of the file, and Parquetry loads it only for the row groups left by the footer statistics.

If your files are read mostly by a reader without page index support, smaller row groups help that reader. --row-group-bytes and --row-group-rows set them, and the page index still serves the readers able to use it.

items.title: Filter rows
items.text:
You want the rows matching a condition without reading the whole file. Pass a predicate to the read: Parquetry skips the parts of the file unable to match, and returns the matching rows. This guide builds predicates, counts the matching rows and shows what a filter skips.

It needs parquetry-core. Getting started adds the dependency and downloads the countries.parquet file used below.

items.title: Filter a read
items.text:
The program prints the countries in Africa or with at least 100 million inhabitants:

import static io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Pred.col;

import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ParquetFileReader;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ReadOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Projection;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.io.ByteRangeSource;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.record.ParquetRecord;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ColumnPath;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class FilterCountries {

    private static final ColumnPath NAME = ColumnPath.of("name");

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Path path = Path.of("countries.parquet");
        Predicate africa = col("continent").eq("Africa");
        Predicate populous = col("pop_est").gtEq(100_000_000.0);
        Predicate filter = africa.or(populous);
        Projection columns = Projection.ofPhysical(List.of(NAME));

        try (ByteRangeSource source = ByteRangeSource.ofFile(path)) {
            ParquetFileReader reader = ParquetFileReader.open(source);
            try (Stream<ParquetRecord> rows = reader.read(filter, columns, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS)) {
                rows.forEach(row -> System.out.println(row.getString(NAME)));
            }
        }
    }
}

It prints Tanzania, W. Sahara and United States of America.

The predicate is evaluated inside the read. A Parquet file stores its rows in blocks called row groups. The footer of the file records the minimum and maximum of the columns of a row group. A row group cuts its columns into pages, and the page index of the file records their minimum and maximum. Parquetry uses these records to skip the row groups and pages that cannot match, then tests the remaining rows one by one. The stream returns only the matching rows. The filter columns do not have to be in the projection.

items.title: Build a predicate
items.text:
Pred.col(name) starts a predicate on a column. Pred.col("a", "b") names the b field of the a struct.

Predicate Builder equal, not equal eq(v), notEq(v) less, less or equal lt(v), ltEq(v) greater, greater or equal gt(v), gtEq(v) in a list of values inInts(...), inStrings(...), inUuids(...) null, not null isNull(), isNotNull() bounding box relations see Filter by location

Combine predicates with and, or and negate on a predicate, or with Pred.and(...), Pred.or(...) and Pred.not(...). Predicate.ALWAYS_TRUE selects the whole file.

The type of the value must match the type of the column:

  • an int or a long for an INT32 or INT64 column;
  • a float or a double for a FLOAT or DOUBLE column;
  • a String for a string column;
  • a LocalDate for a DATE column, a UUID for a UUID column.

A value of another type fails the read with a ParquetSchemaException: col("pop_est").gtEq(100_000_000) passes an int to a DOUBLE column and fails. A predicate on a column absent from the file fails the same way.

The builders take these Java types:

  • eq and notEq take an int, a long, a double or a String. eq also takes a float, a boolean, a binary value, a LocalDate, a LocalDateTime with a flag telling whether the column is adjusted to UTC, and a UUID.
  • lt, ltEq, gt and gtEq take an int, a long or a double. lt and gtEq also take a UUID.

The other comparisons, such as a range of strings or of dates, are records of Predicate, built with a Value:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Value;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ColumnPath;
import java.time.LocalDate;

Predicate fromT = new Predicate.GtEq(ColumnPath.of("name"), new Value.StringVal("T"));
Predicate since2020 = new Predicate.GtEq(ColumnPath.of("opened"), new Value.DateVal(LocalDate.of(2020, 1, 1)));

On countries.parquet, fromT selects Tanzania, United States of America and W. Sahara. since2020 selects the rows opened in 2020 or later, on a file with a DATE column named opened. Value also has records for timestamps, times and decimals.

Float statistics describes how comparisons treat NaN and the two zeros.

items.title: Filter on a list
items.text:
A column inside a list holds several values per row, and a plain comparison has no single answer for them. Wrap the comparison in Predicate.Quantified and say how many elements must match:

import static io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Pred.col;

import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.MatchAction;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;

Predicate taggedPort = new Predicate.Quantified(MatchAction.ANY, col("tags", "list", "element").eq("port"));

MatchAction.ANY keeps a row when at least one element matches, ALL when each element matches, and ONE when exactly one element matches. The path names the leaf of the list in the standard layout: tags.list.element for a list of strings named tags. A comparison on such a column without Quantified fails the read with a ParquetSchemaException.

items.title: Count the matching rows
items.text:
count returns the number of matching rows without building them:

long matches = reader.count(filter, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS);

With the predicate of the first sample, it returns 3. Counting explains how a count answers from statistics where it can.

items.title: See what a filter skips
items.text:
explain runs the pruning tiers on the footer and the indexes, without reading data, and returns the decisions of the tiers, row group by row group:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.explain.ExplainPlan;

ExplainPlan plan = reader.explain(filter, columns, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS);
System.out.println(plan.toAsciiTable());

plan.toJson() renders the same plan as JSON. The par explain command prints it from the command line (Filter rows with par).

items.title: Turn a tier off
items.text:
ReadOptions.DEFAULTS turns the pruning tiers on. The builder turns a tier off for one read, for example to measure what it saves or to work around a file with wrong statistics:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ReadOptions;

ReadOptions options = ReadOptions.builder().useColumnIndexFilter(false).build();
Switch What it turns off useStatsFilter Pruning row groups by the min/max statistics of their columns. useColumnIndexFilter Pruning pages by the page index. A read with this switch off also learns no pages from page headers, and uses none of the pages learned by earlier reads. useBloomFilter Pruning row groups by bloom filters, for eq and in predicates. useRecordLevelFilter Testing the rows one by one. The read then returns the rows of the row groups and pages kept by the other tiers, matching or not. usePageNarrowedFetch Fetching only the surviving pages of a column. The read fetches whole column chunks, the values of a column in a row group, and still skips the pruned pages when decoding.

The pruning tiers skip work. They never change which rows a read returns, as long as the record-level filter stays on.

items.title: Write files that filter well
items.text:
Pruning works from the metadata of the file. A file prunes well when similar values sit together, in the same row groups and pages:

  • Sort the rows by the columns used in filters before writing them.
  • Write a page index. Parquetry's writer writes one by default. Without one, a read learns the pages from their headers, as described in Without a page index.
  • Write bloom filters on the columns compared with eq or in against many distinct values. Write files shows how.

Lay out files for selective queries gives the recommended layout and how to write it.

items.title: Read GeoParquet
items.text:
You have a GeoParquet file and want its geometries as JTS objects, with the coordinate reference system and the extent of the data. This guide reads the geometries of a file, then its GeoParquet metadata: its geometry columns, their coordinate reference system and their extent.

It needs parquetry-core, which includes JTS. Getting started adds the dependency and downloads the countries.parquet file used below.

items.title: Read the geometries
items.text:
The program reads the names and the geometries of the countries, and decodes the geometry with JTS:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ParquetFileReader;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ReadOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Projection;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.geo.MemorySegmentWkbReader;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.io.ByteRangeSource;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.record.ParquetRecord;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ColumnPath;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ParquetSchema;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;
import org.locationtech.jts.geom.Geometry;

public class ReadGeometries {

    record Country(String name, Geometry geometry) {}

    private static final ColumnPath NAME = ColumnPath.of("name");
    private static final ColumnPath GEOMETRY = ColumnPath.of("geometry");
    private static final MemorySegmentWkbReader WKB = new MemorySegmentWkbReader();

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Path path = Path.of("countries.parquet");
        Projection columns = Projection.ofPhysical(List.of(NAME, GEOMETRY));

        try (ByteRangeSource source = ByteRangeSource.ofFile(path)) {
            ParquetFileReader reader = ParquetFileReader.open(source);
            try (Stream<Country> rows =
                    reader.read(Predicate.ALWAYS_TRUE, columns, ReadGeometries::toCountry, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS)) {
                rows.forEach(ReadGeometries::printCountry);
            }
        }
    }

    private static Country toCountry(ParquetSchema schema, ParquetRecord row) {
        String name = row.getString(NAME);
        Geometry geometry = row.readBinary(GEOMETRY, WKB::read);
        return new Country(name, geometry);
    }

    private static void printCountry(Country country) {
        String type = country.geometry().getGeometryType();
        System.out.println(country.name() + ": " + type);
    }
}

It prints Fiji: MultiPolygon, Tanzania: Polygon, and three more lines.

GeoParquet stores a geometry as WKB bytes, the Well-Known Binary encoding of geometries. readBinary hands the bytes of the value to MemorySegmentWkbReader, which decodes them without an intermediate copy. The WKB reader is thread-safe, and one instance can serve concurrent reads. readBinary returns null for a null geometry.

To read whole rows instead, pass a JtsMaterializer as the materializer: new JtsMaterializer(reader.schema()). It returns the rows as Map<ColumnPath, Object> instances, with a JTS Geometry for each geometry column. It sets the SRID of a geometry when the CRS of its column has an EPSG code, and leaves it at 0 otherwise. The other columns hold the values returned by ParquetRecord.get: a string column holds a MemorySegment, not a String. Such a segment is a view over the decoded batch, valid only while the stream hands you the row, as described in Read the values of a row. Decode the needed strings before the stream moves on, or read them with getString in your own materializer, as in the sample above. The geometries are owned JTS objects, safe to keep.

items.title: Find the geometry columns
items.text:
A file declares its geometry columns in two ways. A GeoParquet 1.x file lists them in the geo document of its key/value metadata. A file with the native Parquet geometry types annotates the columns in its schema, and a GeoParquet 2.0 file does both. GeometryColumns reads both declarations:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.geo.geoparquet.GeometryColumns;
import java.util.Set;

Set<ColumnPath> geometryColumns = GeometryColumns.resolve(reader.schema(), reader.keyValueMetadata());

reader.schema() annotates the geometry columns of a GeoParquet 1.x file with the Geometry logical type, as a 2.0 file does. The annotation includes the CRS of the column when the file declares one.

items.title: Read the geo document
items.text:
GeoParquetMetadata.parse reads the geo document into typed records:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.geo.geoparquet.GeoColumn;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.geo.geoparquet.GeoParquetMetadata;

String geoJson = reader.keyValueMetadata().get("geo");
GeoParquetMetadata geo = GeoParquetMetadata.parse(geoJson);
GeoColumn primary = geo.columns().get(geo.primaryColumn());
System.out.println("Geometry types: " + primary.geometryTypes());

For countries.parquet, it prints Geometry types: [Polygon, MultiPolygon]. The record of the column also holds its encoding, its bounding box, and its bbox covering columns when the file has them.

The crs() of a column is a ColumnCrs, with three cases defined by the GeoParquet specification:

  • ColumnCrs.DEFAULTED: the document names no CRS, and the column uses the default, OGC:CRS84.
  • ColumnCrs.UNKNOWN: the document sets the CRS to null. The CRS is unknown, and no default applies.
  • ColumnCrs.Defined: the document holds the CRS as a PROJJSON document. projjson() returns it parsed.

Treat an unknown CRS as unknown. Reading it as OGC:CRS84 would state degrees for coordinates that may be in metres.

items.title: Get the extent
items.text:
bounds returns the bounding box of the primary geometry column over the rows matching a predicate:

import static io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Pred.col;

import io.tileverse.parquetry.format.BoundingBox;
import java.util.Optional;

Optional<BoundingBox> extent = reader.bounds(Predicate.ALWAYS_TRUE, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS);
Optional<BoundingBox> africa = reader.bounds(col("continent").eq("Africa"), ReadOptions.DEFAULTS);

With a filter, the result is the 2D bounding box of the matching geometries. Like count, bounds answers from statistics where it can, and elsewhere decodes only the geometry and the predicate columns. Without a filter, the box comes from the metadata of the file when the file records one, and no row group is read. A row group is a block of rows of the file. The result is empty when the file has no geometry column, or when no matching row has a geometry.

items.title: JSON
items.text:
You want the rows of a Parquet file as JSON, for a web response, a log or a tool reading JSON. parquetry-jackson renders the rows of a read as JSON with Jackson 3, nested columns and Parquet Variant columns included. It is the JSON renderer of the par command line tool.

It needs parquetry-jackson, with the BOM imported as in Getting started:

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.tileverse.parquetry</groupId>
  <artifactId>parquetry-jackson</artifactId>
</dependency>

The module brings Jackson 3 (tools.jackson.core and tools.jackson.databind).

items.title: Read rows as JSON
items.text:
The program prints the North American countries of the countries.parquet file of Getting started, one JSON object per row:

import static io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Pred.col;

import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ParquetFileReader;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ReadOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Projection;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.io.ByteRangeSource;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.jackson.JacksonMaterializers;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.materializer.Materializer;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ColumnPath;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class CountriesAsJson {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Path path = Path.of("countries.parquet");
        Predicate filter = col("continent").eq("North America");
        Projection columns = Projection.ofPhysical(List.of(ColumnPath.of("name"), ColumnPath.of("pop_est")));
        Materializer<String> toJson = JacksonMaterializers.jsonString();

        try (ByteRangeSource source = ByteRangeSource.ofFile(path)) {
            ParquetFileReader reader = ParquetFileReader.open(source);
            try (Stream<String> rows = reader.read(filter, columns, toJson, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS)) {
                rows.forEach(System.out::println);
            }
        }
    }
}

It prints:

{"pop_est":3.7589262E7,"name":"Canada"}
{"pop_est":3.28239523E8,"name":"United States of America"}

JacksonMaterializers.jsonString() is a materializer: the read calls it for each row, as described in Read records, and it returns the row as a compact JSON string. The fields follow the order of the columns in the file. JacksonMaterializers.jsonNode() returns a Jackson JsonNode instead, to read or change before writing it out.

A multi-file dataset takes the same materializers in its read method.

items.title: Write a stream of rows
items.text:
JsonRecordEncoder writes the rows of a read to an OutputStream:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.jackson.JsonRecordEncoder;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.record.ParquetRecord;

Stream<ParquetRecord> rows = reader.read(Predicate.ALWAYS_TRUE, Projection.ALL, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS);
JsonRecordEncoder.writeNdjson(System.out, reader.schema(), rows);
  • writeNdjson writes one JSON object per line (newline-delimited JSON), and writeArray writes the rows as one JSON array.
  • Both read the stream to its end and close it. They leave the output stream open.
  • The schema describes the columns of the rows: with Projection.ALL, it is the schema of the file. For a projection, use a materializer, which receives the projected schema from the read.

JsonRecordEncoder.writeObject(generator, schema, row) writes one row onto a Jackson JsonGenerator of your own, for example to place the rows inside a larger document.

items.title: How values are written
items.text:
Parquet column JSON BOOLEAN boolean INT32, INT64, FLOAT, DOUBLE number binary with the STRING, ENUM or JSON logical type string, the text of the value binary with the UUID logical type string, in the canonical UUID form other binary columns string, the bytes in Base64 struct object list array map with string keys object map with other keys array of {"key": ..., "value": ...} objects Variant the value itself: object, array, string, number, boolean or null

A null field of an object is left out. A null inside a list, or a null map value, is written as null, because its position matters.

Apart from the string and UUID types of the table, values are written by their physical type, without their logical type. A DATE column is the number of days since 1970-01-01, a TIMESTAMP column is a number in the unit of the column, and a DECIMAL column is its unscaled number or, when stored as bytes, Base64. A WKB geometry column is Base64: the countries.parquet file prints its geometry column as a long Base64 string.

items.title: Read columnar batches
items.text:
You process data a column at a time, for example to sum the values of a column, and need no row objects. readBatches returns the matching rows of a file as batches of column vectors. This guide sums a column of the matching rows.

It needs parquetry-core. Getting started adds the dependency and downloads the countries.parquet file used below.

items.title: Sum a column
items.text:
The program adds up the population of the African countries of the file:

import static io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Pred.col;

import io.tileverse.parquetry.columnar.DoubleVector;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.columnar.ParquetRecordBatch;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ParquetFileReader;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ReadOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Projection;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.io.ByteRangeSource;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ColumnPath;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class SumPopulation {

    private static final ColumnPath POPULATION = ColumnPath.of("pop_est");

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Path path = Path.of("countries.parquet");
        Predicate filter = col("continent").eq("Africa");
        Projection columns = Projection.ofPhysical(List.of(POPULATION));

        try (ByteRangeSource source = ByteRangeSource.ofFile(path)) {
            ParquetFileReader reader = ParquetFileReader.open(source);
            try (Stream<ParquetRecordBatch> batches = reader.readBatches(filter, columns, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS)) {
                double total = batches.mapToDouble(SumPopulation::sumPopulation).sum();
                System.out.println("Population of Africa: " + total);
            }
        }
    }

    private static double sumPopulation(ParquetRecordBatch batch) {
        try (batch) {
            DoubleVector population = (DoubleVector) batch.columns().get(POPULATION);
            double sum = 0;
            for (int row = 0; row < batch.rowCount(); row++) {
                if (population.isValid(row)) {
                    sum += population.getDouble(row);
                }
            }
            return sum;
        }
    }
}

It prints Population of Africa: 5.8608716E7.

readBatches takes the same arguments as read: a predicate, a projection and the read options. It applies the predicate exactly. A batch holds only the matching rows, and only the projected columns.

items.title: Read the vectors
items.text:
batch.columns() maps the projected column paths to their ColumnVector. The type of the vector follows the physical type of the column:

Parquet type Vector Value accessor INT32 IntVector getInt(row) INT64 LongVector getLong(row) FLOAT FloatVector getFloat(row) DOUBLE DoubleVector getDouble(row) BOOLEAN BooleanVector getBoolean(row) BYTE_ARRAY, strings included BinaryVector get(row), a MemorySegment struct, list, map StructVector, ListVector, MapVector batch.materialize(row)

A typed accessor throws on a null row: check isNull(row) or isValid(row) first, or use get(row), which returns null for a null row. batch.materialize(row) returns the row as a ParquetRecord, with the accessors described in Read records.

items.title: Close each batch
items.text: Close a batch when you are done with it. Closing releases its off-heap buffers, and a vector backed by them is unreadable afterwards. Read or copy the needed values before closing the batch. Close the stream as well: closing it stops the read. Tune memory sizes the memory held by the reads.

items.title: Options that matter
items.text:
• Batch size. A batch holds at most the rows of one page by default. A page is a run of values of one column, stored and compressed as a unit. ReadOptions.builder().batchSize(1024).build() caps it at 1,024 rows.
  • Filter switches. The pruning switches of Filter rows apply to readBatches as they do to read.

items.title: Read records
items.text:
You have a Parquet file and want its rows as objects of your own Java type, with only the needed columns. This guide reads three columns of a file into a Java record, then shows how to read the values of a row and how long they stay valid.

It needs parquetry-core. Getting started adds the dependency, lists the JVM flags, and downloads the countries.parquet file used below.

items.title: Read the rows into your own type
items.text:
The program reads three columns of the countries into a Java record:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ParquetFileReader;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ReadOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Projection;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.io.ByteRangeSource;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.materializer.Materializer;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.record.ParquetRecord;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ColumnPath;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ParquetSchema;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class ReadCountries {

    record Country(String name, String continent, double population) {}

    private static final ColumnPath NAME = ColumnPath.of("name");
    private static final ColumnPath CONTINENT = ColumnPath.of("continent");
    private static final ColumnPath POPULATION = ColumnPath.of("pop_est");

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Path path = Path.of("countries.parquet");
        Projection columns = Projection.ofPhysical(List.of(NAME, CONTINENT, POPULATION));
        Materializer<Country> toCountry = ReadCountries::toCountry;

        try (ByteRangeSource source = ByteRangeSource.ofFile(path)) {
            ParquetFileReader reader = ParquetFileReader.open(source);
            try (Stream<Country> rows = reader.read(Predicate.ALWAYS_TRUE, columns, toCountry, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS)) {
                List<Country> countries = rows.toList();
                countries.forEach(System.out::println);
            }
        }
    }

    private static Country toCountry(ParquetSchema schema, ParquetRecord row) {
        String name = row.getString(NAME);
        String continent = row.getString(CONTINENT);
        double population = row.getDouble(POPULATION);
        return new Country(name, continent, population);
    }
}

It prints the five countries of the file, from Country[name=Fiji, continent=Oceania, population=889953.0] to Country[name=United States of America, continent=North America, population=3.28239523E8].

A Materializer turns a row into a value of your type. The reader calls it once per row, while the row is readable. Without a materializer, read returns a stream of ParquetRecord, as in Getting started.

items.title: Choose the columns
items.text:
The projection names the columns to decode:

  • Projection.ALL decodes the columns of the file, in schema order.
  • Projection.ofPhysical(List.of(...)) decodes the listed columns, in the listed order.

A column is a ColumnPath. A nested column is named by its full path: ColumnPath.of("address", "city") is the city field of the address struct. A read decodes the projected columns, and also the columns of the predicate, even when the projection leaves them out.

Projecting a column absent from the file fails the read with a ParquetSchemaException.

items.title: Read the values of a row
items.text:
ParquetRecord has two families of accessors:

  • The typed get accessors return values that you can keep: getInt, getLong, getFloat, getDouble, getBoolean, getString, getBinary (a copy of the bytes) and getUuid. They take a ColumnPath, or the position of the column in the projection.
  • The read accessors return views over the decoded batch: readBinary, readStruct, readList and readMap. A view is valid only while the stream hands you the row.

readList returns ParquetRecord elements for a list of structs, and each element names its fields by their name in the struct. For a list of primitive values, the elements are the values themselves: boxed numbers, or a MemorySegment for each string. Read such a list as a List<?>, for example with get(column).

getString and getBinary return null for a null value. A primitive accessor such as getDouble has no null to return: check isNull first on an optional column. isNull also answers true when a struct holding the column is null, and an accessor called on such a column throws. An accessor of the wrong type for the column, such as getInt on a DOUBLE column, throws a ParquetSchemaException.

get(column) returns any value as an Object: a boxed primitive, a MemorySegment for a binary or string column, a java.util.List for a list column, or a ParquetRecord for a struct. Boxed primitives are yours to keep. The MemorySegment, list, map and struct values are views over the batch, like the values of the read accessors: they are valid only while the stream hands you the row. Use getString to read a string column as a String, and getBinary to copy the bytes of a binary column.

items.title: Keep rows
items.text: A row is a view over a batch of decoded rows, and the batch is released as the stream moves on. A materializer that builds its result from owned values, such as the String and double of the sample, needs nothing more. A result holding a view returned by get or by a read accessor is not safe to keep: copy or decode the view inside the materializer. To keep the ParquetRecord itself, call detach(): it copies the values out of the batch.

items.title: Look at the file before reading
items.text:
ParquetFileReader answers from the footer of the file, without reading any data:

  • schema() returns the schema of the file. schema().leafColumns() lists the paths of its columns.
  • rowGroups() lists the row groups, the blocks of rows of the file, with their row counts and sizes.
  • keyValueMetadata() returns the key/value metadata of the file, such as the GeoParquet geo document.

items.title: Options that matter
items.text:
• Opening. ByteRangeSource.ofFile opens a local file. Cloud storage opens a file on an HTTP server or in object storage.
  • Sharing. A ParquetFileReader is safe to share between threads. Open it once per file and run concurrent reads on it. Each read has its own state.
  • Closing. Close the streams returned by read, to release the buffers of the read. Close the ByteRangeSource after the last stream, because the reader does not own it. Tune memory sizes the memory held by the reads.
  • Read options. ReadOptions.DEFAULTS turns on the pruning tiers, the levels at which a filtered read skips parts of the file. Filter rows lists the switches.

  • Multi-file datasets reads a directory of files as one dataset.
  • JSON reads rows as JSON.

items.title: Filter by location
items.text:
You have a GeoParquet file and want the features in an area, such as the map window of a request. A read given a bounding box returns the rows whose geometry has a bounding box overlapping it, and skips the parts of the file whose recorded bounds lie outside it. An exact geometry test, such as a true intersection with a polygon, can run in the same read.

It needs parquetry-core, which includes JTS. Getting started adds the dependency and downloads the countries.parquet file used below.

items.title: Filter by bounding box
items.text:
The program prints the countries whose bounding box overlaps a box around North America:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ParquetFileReader;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ReadOptions;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Bbox;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Pred;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Predicate;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.filter.Projection;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.io.ByteRangeSource;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.record.ParquetRecord;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.schema.ColumnPath;
import java.nio.file.Path;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.stream.Stream;

public class FindByBox {

    private static final ColumnPath NAME = ColumnPath.of("name");

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        Path path = Path.of("countries.parquet");
        Bbox northAmerica = Bbox.of2d(-130, 20, -60, 55);
        Predicate filter = Pred.col("geometry").bboxIntersects(northAmerica);
        Projection columns = Projection.ofPhysical(List.of(NAME));

        try (ByteRangeSource source = ByteRangeSource.ofFile(path)) {
            ParquetFileReader reader = ParquetFileReader.open(source);
            try (Stream<ParquetRecord> rows = reader.read(filter, columns, ReadOptions.DEFAULTS)) {
                rows.forEach(row -> System.out.println(row.getString(NAME)));
            }
        }
    }
}

It prints Canada and United States of America.

Bbox.of2d(minX, minY, maxX, maxY) builds the query box, in the coordinates of the file. Four relations compare the bounding boxes of the geometries with the query box:

Builder Keeps a row when the bounding box of its geometry ... bboxIntersects(box) overlaps the query box bboxContains(box) encloses the query box bboxCoveredBy(box) lies inside the query box bboxEquals(box) equals the query box

A bounding box relation is a predicate like the others. It combines with attribute predicates through and, or and negate, and count takes it as well. The geometry column does not have to be in the projection.

A row with a null geometry matches neither a relation nor its negation. Null geometries explains why.

items.title: Apply an exact geometry test
items.text:
A bounding box relation answers whether two shapes could interact. For the exact answer, push a geometry filter into the read. JtsGeometryFilter tests the geometries with JTS:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.geo.JtsGeometryFilter;
import org.locationtech.jts.geom.Coordinate;
import org.locationtech.jts.geom.GeometryFactory;
import org.locationtech.jts.geom.Point;

GeometryFactory geometries = new GeometryFactory();
Point kansas = geometries.createPoint(new Coordinate(-98.5, 39.5));
JtsGeometryFilter containsKansas = JtsGeometryFilter.intersects(ColumnPath.of("geometry"), kansas);
Predicate filter = Predicate.geometryFilter(containsKansas);

With this filter, the program of the previous section prints United States of America alone. A Parquet file stores its rows in blocks called row groups, and the columns of a row group in smaller runs of values called pages. The reader prunes row groups and pages with a bounding box relation derived from the query, then runs the exact test on the remaining rows.

JtsGeometryFilter has a factory for each relation: intersects, touches, crosses, overlaps, contains, covers, within, coveredBy, disjoint, equalsExact, and dwithin(column, query, distance). The query geometry must be in the coordinate reference system of the file, because the filter does not reproject. disjoint has no bounding box to prune with, and tests the rows of the whole file.

The GeoTools data store pushes the geometry filters of GeoServer requests into the read this way.

The other way to apply the exact test is to filter by the bounding box of the query geometry in the read, and to test the returned rows in your own code, with your own geometry library.

items.title: Make files that filter well
items.text:
A spatial filter skips row groups and pages only when the file records where its geometries are:

  • A file with bbox covering columns, four columns holding the bounding box of each geometry, prunes row groups, and pages when the file has a page index. Parquetry's writer adds both by default, as described in Write a GeoParquet file.
  • A GeoParquet 2.0 file with geometry statistics and without covering columns prunes row groups only.
  • A file with neither prunes nothing. The read tests the geometries one by one, and the result is still exact.

Pruning pays off when nearby geometries sit in the same row groups and pages. Sort the rows by location, for example along a space-filling curve, before writing them. Which path applies details the three cases, and Lay out files for selective queries shows how to write such a file.

items.title: Tune memory
items.text:
You run Parquetry in a Java application with a memory limit, such as a container, and want to check or change how much memory its reads may take. Parquetry sizes its memory budgets from the container limit at startup, and most applications need no setting. This guide shows the budgets, the settings changing them, and the JVM settings beside them.

It needs parquetry-core. Memory explains the budgets and why they follow the container limit.

items.title: See the budgets
items.text:
The default runtime holds the budgets shared by the readers of the process:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.runtime.ParquetRuntime;

public class ShowBudgets {

    public static void main(String[] args) {
        ParquetRuntime runtime = ParquetRuntime.defaultRuntime();
        long fetchMiB = runtime.fetchBudget().capacity() >> 20;
        long decodeMiB = runtime.offHeapDecodeBudget().capacity() >> 20;
        System.out.println("fetch budget: " + fetchMiB + " MiB");
        System.out.println("off-heap decode budget: " + decodeMiB + " MiB");
    }
}

Run with -Dparquetry.io.maxOffHeap=2g, it prints:

fetch budget: 409 MiB
off-heap decode budget: 1024 MiB

The fetch budget bounds the native memory of the column data fetched by the reads, and the off-heap decode budget the native memory of decoded values. Both sit outside the Java heap. When the fetch budget is full, the fetch of the row group being read waits for room, then writes its buffers to a temporary file: the read slows down, and the process keeps its size.

items.title: Change the memory figure
items.text:
By default, the budgets derive from the memory left beside the heap: the container limit minus the maximum heap. The fetch budget takes a fifth of it, and the off-heap decode budget half. These settings replace the figures measured on the machine, as system properties or environment variables, with a size such as 512m or 2g:

System property Environment variable Sets parquetry.io.maxOffHeap PARQUETRY_IO_MAX_OFFHEAP The memory figure used to derive the budgets. It is not a cap: the budgets take their fractions of it. parquetry.io.maxSpill PARQUETRY_IO_MAX_SPILL The disk figure used to derive the spill budget. Spill files may take half of it. By default, it is the free space of the spill directory. parquetry.io.spillDir PARQUETRY_IO_SPILL_DIR The directory of the spill files, java.io.tmpdir by default.

The system property wins over the environment variable. A spill directory on a memory-backed file system, such as a tmpfs volume, counts against the memory limit of the container: choose a directory on disk.

items.title: Give readers a runtime of their own
items.text:
ParquetRuntime.builder() sets the budgets explicitly, and ParquetFileReader.open takes the runtime:

import io.tileverse.parquetry.data.ParquetFileReader;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.runtime.DecodeBudget;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.runtime.FetchBudget;
import io.tileverse.parquetry.runtime.ParquetRuntime;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.Optional;

ParquetRuntime runtime = ParquetRuntime.builder()
        .fetchBudget(FetchBudget.ofBytes(256L << 20))
        .offHeapDecodeBudget(DecodeBudget.ofBytes(512L << 20))
        .decodeBudget(DecodeBudget.ofMaxMemoryFraction(0.25))
        .mandatoryBufferWait(Duration.ofSeconds(1))
        .build();
ParquetFileReader reader = ParquetFileReader.open(source, runtime, Optional.empty());

The third argument supplies the decryption keys of an encrypted file. It stays empty, because Parquetry does not read encrypted files (Format support).

The readers opened with one runtime share its budgets. A reader opened with its own runtime gets its own native budgets, and keeping their sum inside the container is up to you. Build one runtime per process, and share it. The datasets of Multi-file datasets read with the default runtime.

decodeBudget is a share of the Java heap: it bounds the batches decoded ahead of the consumer by a read. It is inside -Xmx and adds nothing to the native memory.

items.title: Spill at once, or wait
items.text:
Two settings of the runtime choose between waiting and spilling to disk:

  • mandatoryBufferWait is the longest wait of a read for room in the fetch budget, 1 second by default. When the wait expires, the read takes a memory-mapped temporary file for its buffer. Duration.ZERO spills at once, without waiting.
  • spillEnabled(false) keeps the batches decoded ahead out of spill files: a batch over the decode budget waits for room instead. It is on by default.

Native memory and spill explains the wait and the spill.

items.title: Size the caches
items.text:
Parquetry keeps two kinds of data in the shared caches of tileverse, both on the Java heap:

  • The parsed footers and the page indexes learned from page headers, in the metadata pool, sized by io.tileverse.cache.metadata.max-size. A budget of 0 keeps neither, and reads then learn no pages.
  • The byte ranges read from remote storage, in the data pool, sized by io.tileverse.cache.data.max-size, when the byte-range cache is on (Cloud storage). A GeoTools data store turns it off with its parameter storage.caching.enabled=false.

The tileverse guide Caching layers gives the defaults and the format of the sizes.

ParquetCaches.clearAll() clears both pools. FooterMetadataCache.clear() drops the footers and the learned page indexes alone.

items.title: Allow native access
items.text:
Start the JVM with --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED. Parquetry allocates its buffers of 64 KiB or more as memory mappings on Linux and macOS, and returns their memory to the system as soon as it frees them. Without the flag, the JDK prints a warning at the first mapping. A JVM started with --illegal-native-access=deny keeps the buffers on malloc.

Mapped memory does not appear in the native memory tracking of the JVM (jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory). SegmentPool.getDefault().stats() reports the memory held by the pool. The system property parquetry.io.mappedBackings=false keeps the buffers on malloc.

items.title: Size the container
items.text:
The peak memory of the process is the maximum heap, plus the two native budgets, plus the decompressed pages of the row groups being decoded, plus the native memory of the JVM itself (Sizing against a container limit). With -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=50, the heap takes half the container and the budgets take at most 35% of it. When you size the container:

  • A heap set above half the container shrinks the budgets with the memory left beside it, and more fetches go to spill files. With a heap close to the container limit, the budgets still derive from an eighth of the container. The heap, the budgets, the decoded pages and the JVM itself may then need more memory than the container allows.
  • The on-heap decode budget is inside -Xmx, and adds nothing to the sum.
  • The heap scratch kept by Parquetry for tileverse readers, such as a PMTiles reader, is inside -Xmx too: at most 32 MiB between uses, released after 30 seconds unused. A row-group fetch uses none.
  • The caches are inside -Xmx: their budgets are shares of the heap (Caching layers gives the defaults).

A read still needs the working set of its current row group on the heap. A row group too large for -Xmx fails the read with an OutOfMemoryError, because the budgets bound speculative work and native buffers, not the current row group. Wide projections over large geometry columns are the case to watch. Raise -Xmx or narrow the projection, rather than the budgets.

items.title: JVM settings beside Parquetry's
items.text:
These settings matter in a container, for the native memory of other users in the same JVM:

  • -XX:TrimNativeHeapInterval=<ms> has the JVM return to the system the memory freed to malloc by other native users, such as zlib, the font engine or the network stack. It does not hold down the peak of a burst: under load, malloc refills within the interval.
  • MALLOC_ARENA_MAX bounds the malloc arenas of glibc for the whole process, at a cost for other libraries allocating heavily in the same JVM.
  • -Djdk.nio.maxCachedBufferSize caps the temporary direct buffer kept per thread by the JDK for channel reads into heap buffers.

items.title: Temporary files of the writer
items.text:
The writer encodes the columns of the current row group into temporary files, and appends the row group to the output when it is complete. WriteOptions.builder().tempDir(path) sets their directory, java.io.tmpdir by default. Each writer creates a private subdirectory there and deletes it when it closes. The directory must exist and be writable.

Like the spill directory, a temporary directory on a memory-backed file system counts against the memory limit of the container.
